doc_description: SEC Form 10-K for The AES Corporation (FY2022) detailing its global pivot to net‑zero power—5.2 GW of renewables signed (12.2 GW backlog; BNEF’s #1 corporate clean energy developer), first‑of‑its‑kind 24/7 carbon‑free power deals and a U.S. green hydrogen JV, accelerated coal retirements (e.g., AES Indiana conversion; Chile “Green Blend”), SBU-by-SBU results across US & Utilities, South America (AES Andes), MCAC’s LNG platform, and Eurasia, plus significant 2022 impairments, comprehensive regulatory/environmental risk disclosures, and audited financials and controls.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC Form 10-K annual report for The AES Corporation for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022.
- Cover information includes: SEC file number (1-12291), Delaware incorporation, Arlington, VA headquarters, contact details, and NYSE listings (AES common stock, AESC corporate units).
- Compliance status and classifications: well-known seasoned issuer, large accelerated filer, compliant with filing and interactive data requirements, auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting, not a shell company, no restatement-related recovery analysis noted.
- Equity details: market value of non-affiliate equity as of June 30, 2022 (~$14.03 billion) and shares outstanding as of February 27, 2023 (668,824,617).
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the 2023 Proxy Statement into Parts II and III.
- Comprehensive table of contents outlining:
  - Part I: Business overview, Risk Factors, Unresolved Staff Comments, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Mine Safety Disclosures.
  - Part II: Market for equity securities and share matters, Selected Financial Data, MD&A (including executive summary, consolidated results, SBU performance analysis, key trends, liquidity/capital resources, critical accounting policies), market risk disclosures, audited financial statements and extensive footnotes.
  - Part III: Corporate governance, directors and executive officers, executive compensation, security ownership, related party transactions, auditor fees and services.
  - Part IV: Exhibits and financial statement schedule, signatures.
- Financial statements and notes cover key areas such as accounting policies, fair value, derivatives and hedging, receivables, investments, goodwill and intangibles, regulatory assets/liabilities, debt, leases, benefit plans, segments/geography, revenue, impairments, income taxes, dispositions/acquisitions, EPS, risks and uncertainties, related parties, quarterly data, and subsequent events.
- Glossary providing definitions of frequently used terms and acronyms, including AES subsidiaries and affiliates, non-GAAP measures (Adjusted EPS, Adjusted PTC), industry and regulatory bodies, environmental and market regulations, and operational terms relevant to the power and energy sector.

- Forward-looking statements safe-harbor notice under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.
- Summary of principal risks that could affect results: macroeconomic conditions (including China), wholesale electricity price volatility and hedging effectiveness, fuel price/availability and logistics with related credit support, access to and cost of capital, inflation/interest rate/FX exposures, liquidity and debt covenant compliance (recourse and non-recourse), ability to upstream cash from subsidiaries, changes to corporate and debt credit ratings, asset purchase/sale execution, market competition, operational reliability and outages, O&M cost management, long-term contracting (PPAs, fuel supply) and counterparty credit risk.
- Additional external risks: weather and hydrological variability (hydro, wind, solar), hurricanes, storms, wildfires, pandemics such as COVID-19, supplier/customer performance, and severe weather/natural disasters.

structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase: In this Annual Report the terms “AES,” “the Company,” “us,” or “we” refer to The AES Corporation and all of its subsidiaries and affiliates, collectively.
structure.summary:
- Defines terminology used throughout the report (AES, the Company, The AES Corporation, Parent Company).
- Provides a forward-looking statements disclaimer under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, noting inherent uncertainties, non-comprehensiveness of listed factors, and no obligation to update.
- Summarizes extensive risk factors that could materially affect results, including:
  - Macroeconomic conditions (global and China-specific), demand for electricity, inflation, interest and foreign exchange rates.
  - Market risks: volatility in electricity and fuel prices, fuel availability and logistics, hedging effectiveness, credit support needs.
  - Financing and liquidity: access to capital markets, refinancing needs, debt covenants (recourse and non-recourse), revolver compliance, ability to upstream cash from subsidiaries, credit rating changes.
  - Operational risks: plant availability, outages, equipment failures, O&M cost management, reliability, competition, ability to secure long-term contracts and manage counterparty credit.
  - External events: weather variability (including hydrology, wind, solar resource), storms, wildfires, natural disasters, pandemics, and global supply-chain disruptions.
  - Development and strategy execution: capital raising for projects, execution of development pipeline, success of renewables and energy storage initiatives, availability of government incentives, ESG strategy execution, technology advancements.
  - Customer and structural factors: changes in customer counts/usage, performance of JVs and equity-method investees not controlled, achieving reasonable rate treatment at utilities.
  - Legal and regulatory: changes in domestic/international energy policy, environmental laws (GHG, emissions, CCR), regulatory oversight, tax law changes and challenges, litigation and investigations.
  - Transactional and financial reporting: acquisition performance, insurance adequacy, pension asset performance and funding obligations, asset impairments/disposals, changes in accounting, corporate governance, and securities law, internal control effectiveness.
  - Human capital and cyber: ability to attract/retain talent, cybersecurity risks, and data privacy.
- References where additional details appear (Item 1A—Risk Factors; Item 3—Legal Proceedings).
- Notes that Item 1—Business will outline company strategy and businesses by strategic business unit with key financial drivers, followed by an Executive Summary.

The excerpt is a forward-looking statements and risk disclosure section from the 2022 Annual Report, outlining numerous factors that could cause actual results to differ from expectations. Key risks span:
- Operational and financial execution: supply chain disruptions; ability to raise capital and execute development projects; performance of acquisitions; insurance adequacy; asset impairments or sales.
- Strategic and market dynamics: success in renewable energy and storage initiatives; reliance on government incentives; ESG execution; technological change; customer count and usage shifts; outcomes at non-controlled JVs and equity investments; utility rate treatment.
- Regulatory and legal environment: changes in international and utility regulations; new energy legislation and oversight; environmental laws (GHG, CCR); tax law changes and challenges; litigation and regulatory investigations; evolving accounting, governance, and securities requirements.
- Controls and people: effectiveness of internal controls over financial reporting; ability to attract and retain talent.
- Cyber and data: cyber-attacks, information security breaches, and data privacy risks.
- Pension and retirement: pension asset value declines, expense increases, and funding obligations.

It clarifies that the list is not comprehensive, references additional details in Item 1A—Risk Factors and later filings, and states no obligation to update forward-looking statements. nodes.title: Executive Summary
nodes.heading: Executive Summary
nodes.start_phrase: Incorporated in 1981, AES is a global energy company accelerating the future of energy.
nodes.summary:
- Forward-looking statements caution and extensive risk disclosures, including risks related to supply chain disruptions, capital raising, renewable and storage project execution, government incentives and policy shifts, ESG execution, technology change, customer trends, joint ventures, utility rate treatment, changing laws and regulations (domestic and international), environmental and GHG rules, tax law changes, litigation, acquisitions, insurance, pensions, asset impairments, accounting and governance changes, internal controls, talent retention, cybersecurity, and data privacy.
- Statement that the company has no obligation to update forward-looking statements.
- Introduction to Item 1—Business, noting strategy by strategic business unit (SBU) and cross-references to Risk Factors and Legal Proceedings.
- Executive summary of AES as a global energy company focused on greener, smarter energy solutions through innovation and operational excellence.
- Strategy centered on leading the transition to zero/low-carbon energy aligned with the Paris Agreement’s net-zero by 2050, leveraging trends in decarbonization, electrification, and digitalization.
- Focus on partnering with large corporate customers to enable their carbon-free electricity goals, emphasizing collaboration and co-creation of tailored solutions and bilateral deals.
- 2022 highlights: recognized by BNEF as the #1 global clean energy developer for corporations; signed 5.2 GW of long-term renewable contracts; built a 12.2 GW contracted project backlog as a driver of future growth.
- Notable innovations and partnerships: 24/7 carbon-free energy agreements for global data centers; partnership with Air Products to develop the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility; initiatives with major South American mining companies to transition to renewables and reduce supply-chain emissions.

nodes.title: Our Strategy
nodes.heading: Our Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: AES is an industry leader in developing and operating the solutions that will enable the transition to zero and low-carbon sources of energy and achievement of the Paris Agreement's goal of net-zero emissions by 2050.
nodes.summary:
- Introduces AES as a global energy company focused on accelerating the transition to greener, smarter energy through innovation, partnerships, and operational excellence.
- Outlines strategy to lead in zero- and low-carbon solutions aligned with Paris net-zero by 2050, capitalizing on decarbonization, electrification, and digitalization.
- Emphasizes partnering with large corporate customers; recognized by BNEF in 2022 as the #1 global clean energy developer for corporations.
- Highlights 2022 commercial progress: 5.2 GW of renewables contracted; backlog reached ~12.2 GW; development pipeline expanded from 55 GW to 64 GW; proactive supply-chain and supplier arrangements; substantial 2023–2025 capex directed to renewables.
- Describes customer co-creation, including first-of-its-kind 24/7 carbon-free energy for data centers and a U.S. green hydrogen project with Air Products (≈1.4 GW of wind/solar; >200 MT/day H2).
- Details sector solutions such as “Green Blend” for mining in South America that integrates renewables with thermal to reduce emissions.
- Addresses utility transitions and Just Transition efforts; AES Indiana targeting retirement of remaining coal by end of 2025 while adding renewables and natural gas.
- Notes innovation engine AES Next, which incubates new technologies and business models to sustain competitive advantage.
- Summarizes 2022 strategic highlights: 5,153 MW of renewables/storage signed (including 2,553 MW in the U.S.); 1,943 MW completed across multiple countries; backlog of 12,179 MW (5,453 MW under construction; 6,726 MW with PPAs); upcoming internal management changes expected to modify reporting segments.
- Provides generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated (including AES Indiana) with diversified fuels; key performance drivers (contract mix, reliability, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, economic activity, fixed-cost control, competition, and U.S. renewable tax credits); sales structure (medium-/long-term contracts vs short-term markets) and use of fuel pass-throughs or hedging when needed.

nodes.title: 2022 Strategic Highlights
nodes.heading: 2022 Strategic Highlights
nodes.start_phrase: •We signed 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage under long-term PPAs, including 2,553 MW of solar, wind and energy storage in the United States.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on decarbonization through solutions like Green Blend, integrating renewables with thermal generation to cut emissions, particularly for mining customers.
- Commitment to a Just Transition for communities and workers affected by fossil facility closures; example: AES Indiana plans to retire remaining coal by end of 2025 while adding renewables and natural gas.
- Expansion of the renewable development pipeline from 55 GW (Jan 2022) to 64 GW (end of 2022) via acquisitions and increased development activities (land, permitting, interconnection).
- Proactive supply-chain and supplier arrangements for late-stage projects to mitigate industry shortages; significant capital expenditures through 2025 dedicated to renewable project development.
- Innovation driven by AES Next, the company’s incubator for new technologies and business models that enable greener energy solutions.
- 2022 strategic results:
  - 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage signed under long-term PPAs (including 2,553 MW in the U.S.).
  - 1,943 MW constructed or acquired and operational across the U.S., Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Chile, and Colombia (primarily wind, solar, and storage).
  - Backlog of 12,179 MW, comprising 5,453 MW under construction and 6,726 MW with signed PPAs not yet under construction.
  - Partnership with Air Products to develop the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility, supported by ~1.4 GW of wind/solar and electrolyzers producing over 200 metric tons per day.
  - Anticipated internal management changes leading to updates in financial reporting segments.
- Generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated portfolio (including AES Indiana), diversified by fuel type.
- Key performance drivers: contract structures, plant reliability/flexibility, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, fixed-cost management, competition, and the ability to complete renewables construction and capture U.S. renewable tax credits.
- Sales and contracting approach: predominance of medium- and long-term contracts versus short-term market sales; fuel-based contracts generally include variable cost pass-throughs or tolling; when pass-throughs are absent, the company hedges or secures fuel supply agreements aligned with contract terms.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.heading: Overview
nodes.start_phrase: We currently own and/or operate a generation portfolio of 32,326 MW, including generation from our integrated utility, AES Indiana.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on accelerating the energy transition with lower-carbon solutions, including a Green Blend offering that integrates renewables with thermal power during select hours to cut emissions, particularly for industrial customers like mining.
- Commitment to a Just Transition for workers and communities impacted by fossil plant closures; AES Indiana plans to retire remaining coal by end of 2025 while adding renewables and natural gas.
- Rapid expansion of renewable development pipeline from 55 GW (Jan 2022) to 64 GW (end of 2022) through acquisitions and increased development (land, permitting, interconnection).
- Proactive supply chain and supplier arrangements to mitigate industry shortages; significant capital expenditures through 2025 directed to renewable project development.
- Innovation driven by AES Next, an internal incubator to develop and scale new technologies and business models for greener energy.
- 2022 strategic results:
  - 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage signed under long-term PPAs, including 2,553 MW in the U.S.
  - 1,943 MW of projects completed or acquired and operational across the U.S., Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Chile, and Colombia.
  - Backlog of 12,179 MW: 5,453 MW under construction and 6,726 MW with signed PPAs not yet under construction.
  - Partnership with Air Products to build the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility, supported by ~1.4 GW of wind/solar and electrolyzers producing over 200 metric tons per day.
  - Anticipated internal management changes that will modify financial reporting segments.
- Generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated (including AES Indiana), diversified by fuel.
- Key performance drivers: contract structures, plant reliability/flexibility, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality/weather, economic activity, fixed-cost control, competition, project execution, and U.S. renewable tax credits.
- Sales model emphasizes medium- and long-term contracts; fuel and variable O&M typically recovered via pass-throughs or tolling. Where not passed through, the company hedges or secures aligned fuel supply agreements.

nodes.title: Generation
nodes.heading: Generation
nodes.start_phrase: We currently own and/or operate a generation portfolio of 32,326 MW, including generation from our integrated utility, AES Indiana.
nodes.summary:
- Emissions reduction and transition strategy: Introduction of the Green Blend offering to integrate renewables with thermal generation during select hours, lowering emissions. Commitment to a Just Transition for workers and communities affected by fossil facility closures. Plan to retire AES Indiana’s remaining coal generation by end of 2025, replacing with new renewables and natural gas.
- Renewable growth and pipeline expansion: Development pipeline expanded from 55 GW to 64 GW in 2022 via acquisitions and intensified development (land, permitting, interconnection). Proactive supplier arrangements to mitigate industry shortages. Majority of capital expenditures through 2025 targeted to renewable project development.
- Innovation and incubation: AES Next serves as the technology and business incubator to identify and develop leading-edge, greener energy solutions for future advantage.
- 2022 strategic highlights:
  - Signed 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage under long-term PPAs, including 2,553 MW in the U.S.
  - Brought online or acquired 1,943 MW of primarily wind, solar, and storage in the U.S., Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Chile, and Colombia.
  - Backlog reached 12,179 MW: 5,453 MW under construction and 6,726 MW with signed PPAs not yet under construction.
  - Announced partnership with Air Products to develop the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility, supported by ~1.4 GW of wind/solar and electrolyzers producing over 200 MT/day.
  - Anticipated internal management changes that will modify financial reporting segments.
- Generation overview: Ownership/operation of 32,326 MW (including AES Indiana), diversified by fuel. Key performance drivers include contract structures, plant reliability/flexibility, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, fixed-cost control, and competition. Renewable performance depends on project delivery and realization of U.S. renewable tax credits.
- Contracting and fuel cost management: Majority of generation sold under medium- to long-term contracts versus short-term market sales. Contracts typically recover variable costs (fuel and variable O&M) via pass-throughs or tolling; where not included, the company hedges or secures fuel/energy supply agreements aligned with contract terms.

nodes.title: Generation - Introduction
nodes.heading: Generation
nodes.start_phrase: We currently own and/or operate a generation portfolio of 32,326 MW, including generation from our integrated utility, AES Indiana.
nodes.summary:
Generation
We currently own and/or operate a generation portfolio of 32,326 MW, including generation from our integrated utility, AES Indiana. Our
generation fleet is diversified by fuel type. See discussion below under Fuel Costs.
Performance drivers of our generation businesses include types of electricity sales agreements, plant reliability and flexibility, availability of
generation capacity to meet contracted sales, fuel costs, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity, fixed-cost management, and
competition. The financial performance of our renewables business is also impacted by our ability to complete construction projects and earn
U.S. renewable tax credits.

nodes.title: Contract Sales
nodes.heading: Contract Sales —
nodes.start_phrase: Most of our generation businesses sell electricity under medium- or long-term contracts ("contract sales") or under short-term agreements in competitive markets ("short-term sales").
nodes.summary:
- Describes AES’s decarbonization initiatives, including its Green Blend product that integrates renewables with thermal generation to lower emissions, and a Just Transition approach for communities and workers affected by fossil plant retirements.
- Notes AES Indiana’s plan to retire remaining coal by end of 2025 while adding renewables and natural gas.
- Outlines renewable growth strategy: development pipeline expanded from 55 GW to 64 GW in 2022 via acquisitions and development (land, permitting, interconnections), proactive supplier arrangements to mitigate shortages, and significant capex through 2025 focused on renewables.
- Highlights innovation through AES Next, the company’s incubator for emerging clean energy technologies and business models.
- 2022 strategic results:
  - 5,153 MW of renewables and storage signed under long-term PPAs (2,553 MW in the U.S.).
  - 1,943 MW placed in service or acquired across the U.S. and Latin America (primarily wind, solar, storage).
  - Backlog of 12,179 MW (5,453 MW under construction; 6,726 MW with signed PPAs).
  - Partnership with Air Products to build the largest U.S. green hydrogen facility, powered by ~1.4 GW of wind/solar and capable of >200 MT/day of green hydrogen.
  - Anticipated internal management changes affecting financial reporting segments.
- Provides a generation overview: 32,326 MW owned/operated (including AES Indiana), diversified by fuel; performance drivers include contract structure, reliability/flexibility, capacity availability, fuel costs, seasonality, economic activity, fixed-cost management, competition, and U.S. renewable tax credits.
- Explains contract sales (medium/long-term) structures that recover variable costs via pass-throughs or hedges, include capacity payments to cover fixed costs and return on capital, align currency of revenues/costs, and hedge interest rate exposure to mitigate price, fuel, FX, and rate risks.
- Details short-term sales in competitive markets, merit-order dispatch, higher sensitivity to market prices, provision of ancillary services, and participation in capacity markets that pay for availability.
- Discusses fuel cost management: long-term supply agreements or hedges for contracted plants, indexation alignment, tolling where offtakers supply fuel; short-term procurement for merchant plants; exposure to commodity price volatility.
- Notes that 46% of AES’s generation capacity is renewable (hydro, solar, wind, storage, biomass, landfill gas) with minimal fuel costs.

nodes.title: Short-Term Sales
nodes.heading: Short-Term Sales —
nodes.start_phrase: Our other generation businesses sell power and ancillary services under short-term contracts with average terms of less than two years, including spot sales, directly in the short-term market or at regulated prices.
nodes.summary:
- Describes how long-term contracts underpin project-level, non-recourse financing and often include capacity payments designed to cover fixed O&M, debt service, and provide a return on capital.
- Explains contract structures that mitigate exposure to power and fuel price volatility, foreign exchange, and interest rate changes by using capacity payments, currency matching of revenues/expenses/debt, and hedging of floating-rate exposure.
- Notes alternative long-term arrangements without significant fuel costs or capacity payments that reference spot prices with pass-through costs to recover fixed and variable costs.
- Details short-term/spot sales in system-operator markets using merit order dispatch, making earnings more sensitive to market power prices.
- Highlights participation in ancillary service markets (e.g., voltage support, frequency regulation, spinning reserves) across the portfolio.
- Outlines regulated capacity markets that pay for availability, typically priced on cost of new entry and reserve margins, supplementing energy revenues.
- Emphasizes plant reliability and operational flexibility to meet contract standards, capture peak prices, and maximize market and ancillary revenues.
- Covers fuel cost management: long-term fuel supply agreements and financial hedges for contracted plants; indexation alignment; tolling where the offtaker supplies fuel; short-term fuel procurement for market-based sales; acknowledges commodity price risk.
- States that 46% of generation capacity is from renewables (hydro, solar, wind, storage, biomass, landfill gas) with minimal fuel costs.

nodes.title: Plant Reliability and Flexibility
nodes.heading: Plant Reliability and Flexibility —
nodes.start_phrase: Our contract and short-term sales provide incentives to our generation plants to optimally manage availability, operating efficiency and flexibility.
nodes.summary:
- The company structures long-term contracts to support non-recourse project financing, with capacity payments designed to cover fixed O&M, debt service, and a return on invested capital, typically denominated in the same currency as costs.
- Contracts and related hedges mitigate exposure to power and fuel price volatility, foreign exchange fluctuations, and interest rate changes; project debt may be a mix of fixed and floating rates with significant hedging.
- Some contracted assets also earn regulated, market-based capacity payments; overall, contracts aim to recover fixed expenses and ensure returns if reliability and efficiency standards are met.
- Short-term sales (average terms under two years) are made into merit-order wholesale markets where prices are set by the marginal unit, making cash flows more sensitive to market price swings.
- The portfolio provides ancillary services (e.g., voltage support, frequency regulation, spinning reserves), and many markets include capacity payments based on plant availability, tied to cost of new entry and reserve margins.
- Operational focus emphasizes plant reliability and flexibility to meet contractual standards, capture peak prices, and maximize ancillary revenues.
- Fuel cost management for thermal plants includes long-term fuel supply agreements, financial hedging, indexation alignment, and tolling arrangements where offtakers supply fuel; short-term sales rely on short-term fuel procurement and are exposed to fuel price volatility.
- 46% of generation capacity is from renewables (hydro, solar, wind, energy storage, biomass, landfill gas) with minimal fuel costs.

nodes.title: Fuel Costs
nodes.heading: Fuel Costs —
nodes.start_phrase: For our thermal generation plants, fuel is a significant component of our total cost of generation.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of contracted sales for generation assets, including capacity payments that cover fixed costs, debt service, and return on capital, often denominated to match cost currencies and frequently hedged for interest rate and FX exposure.
- Explanation of contracts without fuel costs or without capacity payments, structured around long-term spot prices with pass-throughs to align revenues with costs and limit commodity price volatility.
- Description of how commercial arrangements mitigate exposure to power and fuel price changes, currency fluctuations, and interest rate shifts, contingent on meeting reliability and efficiency standards.
- Short-term sales model: merchant sales and ancillary services in system-operator markets using merit-order dispatch; greater earnings sensitivity to market prices; participation in ancillary services and capacity markets with availability-based payments.
- Emphasis on plant reliability, efficiency, and operational flexibility to meet contract standards and capture peak pricing and ancillary revenues.
- Fuel cost management strategies: long-term fuel supply agreements, financial hedging, index-linked arrangements, tolling structures, and short-term procurement for merchant plants; reference to commodity price risk.
- Generation portfolio fuel mix: 46% renewables (hydro, solar, wind, storage, biomass, landfill gas), 32% natural gas (including LNG imports in the Dominican Republic and Panama, otherwise local supply), 20% coal (domestic and international sourcing), and 2% pet coke/diesel/oil.
- Note on global sourcing programs to enhance purchasing power for fuels.
- Impacts of seasonality, weather patterns, renewable resource variability, hydrology, and local economic activity on output, margins, and prices.
- Focus on fixed-cost management across all generation businesses, with recovery of most fixed O&M via contracted capacity payments.
- Competitive dynamics: limited competition under medium- and long-term contracts; market-driven dispatch and prices for short-term sales.
- Utilities segment overview: AES Indiana (integrated utility) and AES Ohio (T&D) in the U.S., plus four distribution utilities in El Salvador; total of 2.6 million customers and 3,495 MW of U.S. utility generation capacity; limited competition in El Salvador with option for large customers to become unregulated.
- Utility business model and performance drivers: regulated rate of return, tariff structures, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability; utility revenues classified as regulated.
- Regulatory framework for rates: allowed return based on regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; “used and useful” asset base; recovery of allowed returns and reasonable expenses through tariffs, which are periodically reviewed and may include pass-throughs for fuel and purchased power.

nodes.title: Seasonality, Weather Variations and Economic Activity
nodes.heading: Seasonality, Weather Variations and Economic Activity —
nodes.start_phrase: Our generation businesses are affected by seasonal weather patterns and, therefore, operating margin is not generated evenly throughout the year.
nodes.summary:
- Fuel mix and sourcing for generation: 32% natural gas (mostly locally sourced; LNG imported for Dominican Republic and Panama), 20% coal (U.S. plants use domestic coal; non-U.S. and Puerto Rico source internationally and locally), 2% pet coke/diesel/oil (oil/diesel sourced locally at international-linked prices; pet coke largely from Mexico and the U.S.); use of a global sourcing program to enhance purchasing power.
- Operational drivers for generation: seasonality and weather variability (temperature, solar, wind, hydrology) affect output and margins; local economic activity influences demand and short-term power prices in competitive markets.
- Cost management: emphasis on managing and reducing fixed O&M costs; in long-term contracted plants, most fixed costs are recovered via capacity payments.
- Competitive dynamics: limited competition during medium- and long-term contract periods; short-term dispatch and prices set by market competition and local reliability rules.
- Utilities portfolio overview: AES operates six utilities—AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. plus four in El Salvador—serving 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation capacity.
- U.S. utility operations: AES Indiana is fully integrated (generation, transmission, distribution); AES Ohio handles transmission and distribution; both are sole distributors in their jurisdictions.
- El Salvador utilities: limited competition due to high entry barriers; large regulated customers may opt to become unregulated and procure directly from generators or marketers.
- Utility performance drivers: regulated rate of return and tariffs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability; utility revenues classified as regulated.
- Regulation and tariffs: regulators set tariff frameworks and service standards; utilities earn an allowed return based on a defined regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; allowed returns and reasonable operating expenses are recovered through tariffs.
- Tariff mechanics: subject to periodic review/reset; typically usage-based and may include pass-through of non-controllable costs (e.g., fuel for integrated utilities and purchased energy).

nodes.title: Fixed-Cost Management
nodes.heading: Fixed-Cost Management —
nodes.start_phrase: In our businesses with long-term contracts, the majority of the fixed O&M costs are recovered through the capacity payment.
nodes.summary:
- Fuel mix and sourcing: 32% of generation capacity fueled by natural gas (mostly locally sourced; LNG imports in Dominican Republic and Panama); 20% coal (domestic in U.S., mix of international/local elsewhere, including Puerto Rico); 2% pet coke, diesel or oil (oil/diesel sourced locally at international-linked prices; pet coke largely from Mexico and the U.S.); use of a global sourcing program to optimize fuel procurement.
- Operational drivers: seasonality and weather variability affect margins and renewable output (temperature, solar/wind resources, hydrology); local economic activity influences demand and power prices in competitive markets.
- Cost management: in long-term contracted generation, fixed O&M largely recovered via capacity payments; ongoing fixed-cost reduction is a key performance driver across generation.
- Competition: limited during medium/long-term contract terms; short-term sales subject to market competition and dispatch/reliability rules.
- Utility portfolio: AES operates six utilities—AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. plus four in El Salvador—serving 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation.
- U.S. utility roles: AES Indiana is fully integrated (generation, transmission, distribution); AES Ohio is a transmission and distribution regulated utility; both are sole distributors in their territories.
- El Salvador utilities: limited competition due to entry barriers; large regulated customers may opt out to buy directly from generators/commercializers.
- Utility revenue model and regulation: revenues classified as regulated; tariffs and service standards set by regulators; utilities earn an allowed rate of return based on regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; reasonable O&M and allowed returns recovered through tariffs, which are periodically reviewed and may include pass-throughs for fuel or purchased energy costs.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.heading: Competition —
nodes.start_phrase: For our businesses with medium- or long-term contracts, there is limited competition during the term of the contract.
nodes.summary:
- Fuel mix and sourcing: 32% of generation capacity is natural-gas fired (primarily locally sourced; LNG imported for Dominican Republic and Panama), 20% coal (U.S. plants use domestic coal; non-U.S. and Puerto Rico source internationally; global sourcing used to optimize procurement), and 2% pet coke/diesel/oil (oil and diesel sourced locally at international-linked prices; pet coke mainly from Mexico and the U.S.).
- Operating drivers: Seasonality and weather (temperature, wind/solar resources, hydrology) affect output and margins, especially for renewables; local economic activity influences demand and short-term power prices in competitive markets.
- Cost management: In long-term contracted generation, capacity payments recover most fixed O&M; across all generation businesses, reducing fixed costs remains a key performance lever.
- Competition: Limited during medium- and long-term contract periods; short-term sales subject to market competition and dispatch/reliability rules.
- Utilities overview: Six utilities (AES Indiana, AES Ohio, and four in El Salvador) serve 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation. AES Indiana is fully integrated (generation, transmission, distribution); AES Ohio is transmission and distribution only. El Salvador distribution faces limited competition; large regulated customers may opt to become unregulated and buy directly from generators/marketers.
- Utility revenue and performance: Utility revenues are regulated. Key drivers include allowed rate of return and tariff design, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability.
- Regulation and tariffs: Regulators set tariffs and service standards. Utilities earn a regulated return on an allowed regulatory asset base (assets deemed used and useful), considering capital structure and cost of capital. Tariffs recover the allowed return and reasonable operating expenses, are periodically reviewed/reset, are typically usage-based, and often include pass-through mechanisms for uncontrollable costs such as fuel and purchased power.

nodes.title: Utilities
nodes.heading: Utilities

- Competition: Limited during medium- and long-term contracts; short-term sales subject to market competition and dispatch/reliability rules.
- Utilities overview: AES operates AES Indiana (fully integrated) and AES Ohio (transmission and distribution) in the U.S., plus four distribution utilities in El Salvador; serves approximately 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation; sole distributors in their jurisdictions; limited competition in El Salvador, though large regulated customers may opt to become unregulated and buy directly from generators/commercializers.

nodes.title: Utilities - Introduction
nodes.heading: Utilities
nodes.start_phrase: Our utility businesses consist of AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. and four utilities in El Salvador.
nodes.summary: AES’s Utilities segment includes AES Indiana, AES Ohio, and four distribution utilities in El Salvador, serving 2.6 million customers; the two U.S. utilities also have 3,495 MW of generation capacity. AES Indiana is a fully integrated utility (generation, transmission, distribution), and AES Ohio operates transmission and distribution; both are sole distributors in their jurisdictions. In El Salvador, distribution faces limited competition due to market entry barriers, though regulation allows large regulated customers to become unregulated users and contract directly with generators or commercialization agents. Utilities sell and bill end-users directly, with key performance drivers including regulated rate of return, tariffs, seasonality, weather, economic activity, and service reliability; utility revenue is classified as regulated on the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

nodes.title: Regulated Rate of Return and Tariff
nodes.heading: Regulated Rate of Return and Tariff —
nodes.start_phrase: In exchange for the right to sell or distribute electricity in a service territory, our utility businesses are subject to government regulation.
nodes.summary:
- Generation fuel mix and sourcing: 32% natural gas (mostly local gas; LNG imports in Dominican Republic and Panama), 20% coal (U.S. plants use domestic coal; non-U.S. and Puerto Rico source internationally and locally with global procurement), 2% pet coke/diesel/oil (oil/diesel priced to international markets; pet coke mainly from Mexico and the U.S.).
- Operating drivers for generation: seasonality and weather impact output and margins, especially for renewables; local economic activity influences demand and short-term prices; fixed-cost management is critical, with fixed O&M largely recovered via capacity payments in long-term contracts; competition limited under medium/long-term contracts, market-based for short-term sales.
- Utilities footprint and model: AES operates AES Indiana (integrated) and AES Ohio (T&D) in the U.S. plus four distribution utilities in El Salvador, serving 2.6 million customers; U.S. utilities include 3,495 MW of generation. Limited competition in El Salvador; large customers can opt out to unregulated service.
- Utility revenue and performance: revenue is regulated; regulators set tariffs and service standards. Allowed return based on regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital; tariffs recover allowed return and reasonable O&M, with pass-through mechanisms for fuel/purchased power. Some high-demand customers may be unregulated but pay non-bypassable distribution fees. Utilities must manage costs to tariff levels, address uncollectibles, and control losses.
- Utility operating factors: margins affected by seasonality and weather; sales influenced by customer count, temperature deviations, economic conditions, energy efficiency, and distributed generation; reliability standards apply, with potential incentives or penalties tied to outage duration and frequency.
- Development and construction: AES develops new generation and utility assets/retrofits to meet customer needs or regulatory requirements, prioritizing renewables in key growth markets. Investment decisions weigh strategic fit and risk-adjusted returns versus alternative uses of capital. The company often secures long-term offtake contracts pre-construction, seeks non-recourse project financing and partners, and uses third-party EPC with in-house construction oversight on budget, safety, and productivity.
- Segment structure and performance metric: operations organized into four SBUs—US and Utilities; South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil); MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean); and Eurasia (Europe, Asia). Two business lines: generation across all SBUs and utilities primarily in US and Utilities; utilities may also participate in wholesale markets. Performance measured by Adjusted PTC (non-GAAP), with SBU-level contributions referenced to the MD&A.

nodes.title: Seasonality, Weather Variations, and Economic Activity
nodes.heading: Seasonality, Weather Variations, and Economic Activity —
nodes.start_phrase: Our utility businesses are generally affected by seasonal weather patterns and, therefore, operating margin is not generated evenly throughout the year.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory framework and tariffs: Explanation of how utility customer rates are set via summary regulatory processes or formula mechanisms; treatment of large-demand customers who may be unregulated but pay non-bypassable distribution fees; emphasis that regulated tariffs are designed to recover operating and fixed costs, manage uncollectibles, service quality, and technical/non-technical losses; utilities must control costs to avoid under-recovery or reduced returns.
- Demand drivers and seasonality: Discussion of how seasonal weather patterns, temperature deviations, customer counts, historic usage, local economic activity, energy efficiency, and distributed generation affect retail sales and operating margins.
- Reliability standards: Utilities are required to meet explicit or implicit reliability metrics (outage duration/frequency) with potential incentives or penalties tied to performance.
- Development and construction strategy: Approach to building or retrofitting generation assets for utility needs or regulatory compliance; requirement for regulatory approvals to ensure capital recovery and returns; focus on developing renewable projects in key growth markets leveraging global scale; investment decisions based on strategic fit, risk-adjusted returns, and alternative capital uses; use of long-term offtake contracts, non-recourse project financing, and partnerships to limit parent equity; third-party construction with internal oversight on budget, safety, efficiency, and productivity.
- Segment organization: Company structured into four SBUs by geography—US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia); two business lines—generation (all SBUs) and utilities (US and Utilities SBU) covering generation/purchase, distribution, transmission, and retail sales, with some wholesale activity.
- Performance measurement: Use of Adjusted PTC (a non-GAAP metric) to assess SBU operating performance, with 2022 contributions by SBU referenced and reconciliation/definitions provided in the MD&A.

nodes.title: Reliability of Service
nodes.heading: Reliability of Service —
nodes.start_phrase: Our utility businesses must meet certain reliability standards, such as duration and frequency of outages.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory framework and tariffs: Utilities recover operating and fixed costs through regulated tariffs, which may include mechanisms for adjusting prices and recovering uncollectible amounts, service quality, and system losses. Some high-demand customers are unregulated, can contract directly with utilities or other suppliers, and pay non-bypassable distribution fees. Utilities must control costs to levels reflected in tariffs to avoid non-recovery or reduced returns.
- Seasonality and demand drivers: Utility margins vary with seasonal weather patterns. Weather deviations, customer counts, temperature variance, historical usage, local economic activity, energy efficiency, and distributed generation all influence retail sales after weather normalization.
- Reliability obligations: Utilities must meet explicit or implicit reliability standards regarding outage duration and frequency, with potential incentives or penalties tied to performance.
- Development and construction strategy: The company develops new generation and retrofits plants to meet customer needs or regulatory requirements, typically seeking regulatory approval to ensure capital recovery and returns for utility projects. For generation growth, focus is on key markets and renewables, evaluating investments against risk-adjusted returns and alternative capital uses. The company often secures long-term offtake contracts prior to construction, pursues non-recourse project financing and partnerships to limit parent equity, and uses third-party EPC with internal oversight of safety, budget, and productivity.
- Organizational structure and segments: Operations are managed through four SBUs—US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia). Two lines of business: generation (all SBUs) and utilities (primarily US and Utilities), with utilities also able to sell into wholesale markets in some cases.
- Performance measurement: SBU operating performance is tracked using Adjusted PTC, a non-GAAP metric, with contributions shown by SBU for 2022 and reconciliations provided elsewhere in the Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Segments
nodes.heading: Segments
nodes.start_phrase: The segment reporting structure uses the Company's management reporting structure as its foundation to reflect how the Company manages the businesses internally and is mainly organized by geographic regions which provides a socio-political-economic understanding of our business.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory environment and tariffs: Utilities operate under regulated tariff frameworks designed to recover operating and fixed costs, uncollectible amounts, quality of service, and technical/non-technical losses. Some jurisdictions allow automatic or formula-based adjustments. Large-demand customers may be unregulated, can contract directly with utilities or alternative suppliers, and pay non-bypassable distribution fees. Utilities must control costs to tariffed levels to avoid non-recovery or reduced returns.
- Seasonality and demand drivers: Earnings are seasonally affected by weather; margins vary during the year. Weather, customer counts, temperature deviations, and historical usage patterns influence results. Weather-adjusted retail sales are impacted by local economic activity, energy efficiency, distributed generation, and customer growth.

Generation growth prioritizes renewables in key markets leveraging scale. Investment decisions weigh strategic fit, risk-adjusted returns, and alternative capital uses. The company often secures long-term offtake contracts before construction, pursues non-recourse project financing and partners to limit parent equity, and uses third-party constructors under internal oversight for safety, budget, and productivity.

nodes.title: Key Financial Drivers
nodes.heading: Key Financial Drivers —
nodes.start_phrase: AES Indiana's financial results are driven primarily by retail demand, weather, and maintenance costs.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Overview of AES Indiana within AES’s US and Utilities businesses, including service territory, generation portfolio, regulatory environment, financial drivers, capital plans, and resource planning.
- Business description: IPALCO’s principal subsidiary AES Indiana is an integrated electric utility serving Indianapolis and nearby areas (exclusive service right over ~528 square miles; ~971,000 population). Owns four Indiana generating stations: Petersburg (coal; Unit 1—230 MW—retired May 31, 2021; Unit 2—415 MW—planned retirement in 2023; remaining coal units to be converted to natural gas by end of 2025), Harding Street (natural gas/fuel oil CTs plus 20 MW battery for frequency response), Eagle Valley (CCGT natural gas), and Georgetown (small gas peaker).
- Renewables and storage: Long-term contracts for 300 MW wind and 94 MW solar. Petersburg Solar Project (250 MW solar + 180 MWh storage), expected 2025 completion subject to IURC approval. Hardy Hills Solar Energy LLC (195 MW solar), expected 2024 completion subject to IURC approval.
- Key financial drivers: Retail demand, weather, maintenance costs, regulatory outcomes, legislative/regulatory changes, and timely recovery of capital expenditures.
- Regulatory framework and rates: Comprehensive IURC regulation over services, facilities, retail rates, securities, etc. Tariff structure includes base rates and multiple riders: fuel and purchased power (Fuel Adjustment Charge), environmental compliance (with return), RTO cost recovery, sharing of wholesale and capacity margins vs. benchmarks, TDSIC investments (return on/return of), and DSM energy efficiency cost/lost margin/performance incentives. Riders are reviewed periodically; overall rates reviewed with base rate cases.
- Recent base rate order: 2018 IURC order increased annual revenues by $44 million (3%), enabling recovery for the Eagle Valley CCGT and other projects; provided ~$50 million of customer benefits over two years.
- Market operations: Member of MISO; AES Indiana’s assets are dispatched by MISO; participates in day-ahead and real-time markets.
- Development strategy: Capital spending for prudent operations, environmental compliance, and discretionary upgrades to replace aging assets and improve performance.
- TDSIC mechanism: Indiana statute enabling recovery outside base rates for eligible T&D and storage projects via a 5–7 year plan; 80% recovered through periodic adjustments (including return, AFUDC, carrying charges, O&M, depreciation, property taxes), 20% deferred to next base rate case; annual increase capped at 2% of total retail revenues. IURC approved AES Indiana’s seven-year, $1.2 billion TDSIC plan (2020–2026). Annual filings since June 2020; as of Dec 31, 2022, $324 million of equipment approved for TDSIC recovery.
- Integrated Resource Plan (Dec 2022): Presents a Preferred Resource Portfolio characterized as the reasonable least-cost approach that delivers a cleaner, more diverse generation mix to meet retail capacity needs over the coming years.

nodes.title: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure
nodes.heading: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
nodes.start_phrase: AES Indiana is subject to comprehensive regulation by the IURC with respect to its services and facilities, retail rates and charges, the issuance of long-term securities, and certain other matters.
nodes.summary:

- Explains AES Indiana’s regulatory oversight by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC), including rate-setting based on allowable costs and a fair return on used-and-useful assets.
- Describes tariff structure: base rates plus multiple riders for fuel and purchased power (Fuel Adjustment Charge), environmental compliance cost recovery (with return), RTO cost changes, sharing of wholesale and capacity margins versus benchmarks, TDSIC returns on/of eligible investments, and demand-side management cost recovery with lost margins and incentives; riders are periodically reviewed.
- Notes the 2018 Base Rate Order: a $44 million (3%) annual revenue increase effective December 5, 2018, primarily to recover Eagle Valley CCGT and other project costs; also provided about $50 million in customer benefits over two years; remains the most recent base rate order.
- Outlines market participation: AES Indiana is a transmission owner in MISO; MISO dispatches generation and operates day-ahead and real-time markets in which AES Indiana offers electricity.
- Summarizes development strategy focused on necessary capital investments for reliability, environmental compliance, modernization, and replacing aging assets.
- Details Indiana’s TDSIC statute enabling recovery for eligible transmission, distribution, and storage projects via a periodic mechanism: 5–7 year plans; 80% of costs (including return, AFUDC, post-in-service carrying charges, O&M, depreciation, property taxes) recovered through riders; 20% deferred to next base rate case; capped at 2% of total retail revenues annually.
- Reports IURC approval (March 4, 2020) of AES Indiana’s seven-year TDSIC Plan totaling $1.2 billion (2020–2026), with annual TDSIC rate adjustments (effective each November) and staggered annual plan updates; $324 million of equipment approved for TDSIC recovery as of December 31, 2022.
- Notes the December 2022 Integrated Resource Plan filing, presenting a Preferred Resource Portfolio aimed at least-cost service with a cleaner, more diversified generation mix to meet future capacity needs.

nodes.title: Development Strategy
nodes.heading: Development Strategy —
nodes.start_phrase: AES Indiana's construction program is composed of capital expenditures necessary for prudent utility operations and compliance with environmental regulations, along with discretionary investments designed to replace aging equipment or improve overall performance.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory context: AES Indiana operates under comprehensive IURC oversight covering services, facilities, retail rates, long‑term securities, and related matters. Rates comprise base tariffs plus multiple riders, with recurring reviews and overall structure examined during base rate cases.
- Rate mechanisms: Riders address fuel and purchased power costs (Fuel Adjustment Charge), environmental compliance recovery (with return), RTO cost changes, sharing of wholesale and capacity margins vs. benchmarks, TDSIC investments (return on and of), and demand-side management cost recovery, lost margins, and incentives.
- 2018 base rate order: IURC approved a $44 million (3%) annual revenue increase, largely for the Eagle Valley CCGT and other projects, effective December 5, 2018, and provided about $50 million of customer benefits over two years via a rate adjustment.
- Market participation: AES Indiana is a transmission owner in MISO, which dispatches generation regionally; the company sells into MISO’s day‑ahead and real‑time markets.
- Capital strategy: Focus on necessary and discretionary investments for reliability, environmental compliance, asset replacement, and performance improvement.
- TDSIC framework: Indiana statute enables recovery of eligible transmission, distribution, and storage investments outside base cases via a periodic adjustment—80% recovered contemporaneously (including return, AFUDC, post‑in‑service carrying charges, O&M, depreciation, and property taxes), 20% deferred to next base rate case; capped at 2% of total retail revenues annually; plans must span 5–7 years.
- TDSIC approvals: IURC approved a seven‑year, $1.2 billion plan (2020–2026). AES Indiana files annual TDSIC rate adjustments and staggered plan updates; $324 million of equipment had been approved for TDSIC recovery as of December 31, 2022.
- Integrated Resource Plan (2022): Filed an IRP identifying a preferred, reasonable least‑cost portfolio to meet capacity needs, aiming for a cleaner, more diverse generation mix for customers.

nodes.title: Integrated Resource Plan
nodes.heading: Integrated Resource Plan —
nodes.start_phrase: In December 2022, AES Indiana filed its Integrated Resource Plan ("IRP"), which describes AES Indiana's Preferred Resource Portfolio for meeting generation capacity needs for serving AES Indiana's retail customers over the next several years.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on AES Indiana’s regulatory environment, rates, and investment recovery mechanisms under the IURC, including multiple riders (fuel, environmental compliance, RTO costs, wholesale/capacity margin pass-throughs, TDSIC, and demand-side management incentives) and periodic reviews.
- Summary of the 2018 Base Rate Order: $44 million annual revenue increase (~3%), recovery for the Eagle Valley CCGT and other projects, effective December 5, 2018, plus ~$50 million in customer benefits over two years.
- AES Indiana’s participation in MISO’s day-ahead and real-time markets and MISO’s dispatch role.
- Development strategy emphasizing required and discretionary capital investments for reliability, modernization, and environmental compliance.
- Details of Indiana’s TDSIC statute: 5–7 year plans, 80% cost recovery via periodic adjustments (including return and various carrying costs), 20% deferred to next base case, with a 2% annual revenue cap.
- Approval of AES Indiana’s seven-year, $1.2 billion TDSIC plan (2020–2026); annual filings and updates; $324 million of equipment approved for recovery as of December 31, 2022.
- 2022 Integrated Resource Plan: preferred least-cost, cleaner portfolio; plan to convert Petersburg Units 3 and 4 from coal to natural gas by end of 2025 (approvals pending); add up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery storage by 2027; monitor emerging technologies (green hydrogen, SMRs, carbon capture).
- 2019 IRP actions: retirement of Petersburg Unit 1 (May 31, 2021) and planned retirement of Unit 2 in 2023; IURC approval for creation and recovery of regulatory assets tied to these retirements.
- Renewable and storage projects: acquisition of 195 MW Hardy Hills Solar (operations expected 2024) and 250 MW Petersburg Solar plus 180 MWh storage (operations expected 2025), both IURC-approved.
- Equity funding: $275 million (2021) and $253 million (2022) from AES and CDPQ to support TDSIC and replacement generation projects.
- Transition to AES Ohio: business overview of a T&D utility serving ~536,000 customers in West Central Ohio; complete exit from generation by 2020.
- AES Ohio key financial drivers: retail demand, weather, regulatory outcomes, legislative changes, and timely T&D cost recovery.
- AES Ohio regulatory framework under PUCO: competitive retail generation via CRES, SSO supply procured through auctions with AES Ohio as default provider, exclusive utility rights for T&D, cost-based distribution ratemaking with allowed returns, and rate mechanisms including timely recovery of power purchase costs.

nodes.title: AES Ohio
nodes.heading: AES Ohio
nodes.start_phrase: DPL is a holding company whose principal subsidiary is AES Ohio.
nodes.summary:
- AES Indiana plans to transition generation by converting Petersburg coal units 3 and 4 to natural gas by end of 2025 (regulatory approvals from the IURC to be sought) and adding up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery storage by 2027; it will evaluate emerging technologies such as green hydrogen, small modular reactors, and carbon capture as they become cost-effective.
- AES Indiana’s 2019 IRP included retiring Petersburg Unit 1 (230 MW) on May 31, 2021, and planning to retire Unit 2 (415 MW) in 2023. The IURC approved creation and amortization of regulatory assets for these retirements, with recovery via future rate cases and parties’ rights reserved on ratemaking details.
- Project development: acquisition of the 195 MW Hardy Hills Solar Project (IURC-approved June 2021; expected online 2024) and an agreement to acquire the 250 MW Petersburg Solar Project with 180 MWh storage (IURC-approved November 2021; expected online 2025).
- Financing: equity contributions of $275 million (December 2021) and $253 million (2022) from AES and CDPQ to fund TDSIC and replacement generation projects.
- AES Ohio overview: DPL’s principal subsidiary; a regulated utility serving approximately 536,000 customers in West Central Ohio; exclusive T&D provider; procures Standard Service Offer (SSO) supply via competitive auctions; exited generation with last asset retired/sold in 2020.
- AES Ohio key financial drivers include retail demand, weather, regulatory outcomes, legislative/regulatory changes, and timely recovery of T&D expenditures.
- Regulatory framework: PUCO regulates distribution services, retail rates and charges, reliability, RPS and energy efficiency compliance. Ohio allows retail choice via CRES providers; SSO supply comes from third parties through auctions, with AES Ohio as provider of last resort. Distribution rates are set through cost-based ratemaking with an authorized return on the regulated asset base, and retail rates include mechanisms for timely recovery of purchased power costs.

nodes.title: Business Description

nodes.title: Key Financial Drivers

nodes.title: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure
nodes.heading: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
nodes.start_phrase: AES Ohio is regulated by the PUCO for its distribution services and facilities, retail rates and charges, reliability of service, compliance with renewable energy portfolio requirements, energy efficiency program requirements, and certain other matters.
nodes.summary:
- AES Indiana transition and resource plan: convert Petersburg coal units 3 and 4 to natural gas by end of 2025 (IURC approvals to be sought), add up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery storage by 2027, and evaluate emerging technologies (green hydrogen, small modular reactors, carbon capture) as they become cost‑effective.
- Petersburg retirements and regulatory treatment: Unit 1 (230 MW) retired May 31, 2021; Unit 2 (415 MW) planned retirement in 2023. IURC approved creation and amortization of regulatory assets for Units 1 and 2 with recovery through future rate cases; parties’ rights on ratemaking treatment reserved.
- Renewable project acquisitions: Hardy Hills Solar (195 MW) acquired Dec 2021, operations expected 2024; Petersburg Solar (250 MW + 180 MWh storage) agreement July 2021, operations expected 2025; both approved by IURC in 2021.
- Equity funding: $275 million (2021) and $253 million (2022) capital contributions from AES and CDPQ to support TDSIC and replacement generation projects.
- AES Ohio business profile: regulated T&D utility serving ~536,000 customers in West Central Ohio; exited generation by 2020; SSO supply procured via competitive auctions; member of PJM RTO.
- Key financial drivers for AES Ohio: retail demand and weather, regulatory outcomes, new legislation/regulations, and timely recovery of T&D expenditures.
- Regulatory framework: PUCO regulates distribution rates, SSO, reliability, portfolio/efficiency requirements; FERC regulates transmission rates. Ohio allows CRES choice; utilities must serve SSO customers and act as provider of last resort.
- Transmission formula rate: filed March 2020, effective May 3, 2020; uncontested settlement approved by FERC April 15, 2021.
- ESP matters: reversion to ESP 1 approved Dec 18, 2019, reinstating non‑bypassable RSC Rider (~$79M annually); OCC appeal to Ohio Supreme Court pending with potential adverse impacts. ESP 4 filed Sept 26, 2022 proposes grid reliability upgrades, proactive vegetation management, customer programs (renewables, EVs, energy efficiency), recovery of outstanding regulatory assets, and excludes the RSC; PUCO approval anticipated in 2023.
- Distribution rate case: filed Nov 30, 2020; PUCO order Dec 14, 2022 authorizes $76M revenue increase, 9.999% ROE, 4.4% long‑term debt cost, $783M rate base, and 53.87% equity/46.13% debt capital structure; effectiveness tied to new ESP approval.
- Smart Grid and comprehensive settlement: Oct 23, 2020 stipulation covering Smart Grid Plan and SEET/MFA findings; PUCO approved June 2021; AES contributed $150M in 2021 for grid modernization; rehearings denied Dec 1, 2021; OCC appeal pending.
- Decoupling and riders: Jan 23, 2020 filing to defer decoupling costs (effective Dec 18, 2019); hearing May 4, 2021; recovery proposed via a new rider in ESP 4.
- Development strategy: continued investment in and upgrades to AES Ohio’s transmission and distribution infrastructure, subject to ongoing reviews and changing conditions.

nodes.title: Smart Grid and Comprehensive Settlement
nodes.heading: Smart Grid and Comprehensive Settlement —
nodes.start_phrase: On October 23, 2020, AES Ohio entered into a Stipulation and Recommendation (settlement) with the staff of the PUCO and various customers, and organizations representing customers of AES Ohio and certain other parties with respect to, among other matters, AES Ohio's applications pending at the PUCO for (i) approval of AES Ohio's plan to modernize its distribution grid (the "Smart Grid Plan"), (ii) findings that AES Ohio passed the Significantly Excessive Earnings Test ("SEET") for 2018 and 2019, and (iii) findings that AES Ohio's current ESP 1 satisfies the SEET and the more favorable in the aggregate ("MFA") regulatory test.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of AES Ohio’s regulatory environment and market participation, including membership in PJM RTO, FERC-regulated transmission rates, and PJM’s administration of energy, ancillary services, and capacity markets.
- Transmission rate developments: formula-based transmission rate approved effective May 3, 2020; uncontested settlement approved by FERC on April 15, 2021.
- State rate framework: PUCO-approved reversion to ESP 1 (Dec 18, 2019), reinstating the non-bypassable Rate Stabilization Charge (about $79 million annually); OCC appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court seeking reversal and potential refund of RSC revenues from August 2021, with possible material adverse impacts if unfavorable.
- New Electric Security Plan (ESP 4) filed Sept 26, 2022: proposes grid upgrades, reliability improvements, price stability measures, economic development investments, increased distribution spending, proactive vegetation management, and new customer programs (renewables, EVs, and energy efficiency for residential/low-income customers); seeks recovery of certain regulatory assets; does not continue the RSC; awaiting PUCO approval (anticipated 2023).
- Distribution rate case: filed Nov 30, 2020; PUCO order issued Dec 14, 2022 authorizing a $76 million revenue increase, 9.999% ROE, 4.4% long-term debt cost, $783 million rate base, and 53.87% equity/46.13% long-term debt capital structure; increase to take effect upon approval of a new ESP (anticipated 2023).
- Smart Grid and Comprehensive Settlement: Oct 23, 2020 settlement addressing the Smart Grid Plan and SEET/MFA findings; PUCO approved in June 2021; AES contributed $150 million in 2021 for infrastructure and grid modernization; rehearing requests denied Dec 1, 2021; OCC appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court filed Dec 6, 2021, pending.
- Decoupling costs: Jan 23, 2020 filing to defer decoupling costs effective Dec 18, 2019 to mitigate impacts of weather, energy efficiency, and economic demand changes; evidentiary hearing held May 4, 2021; recovery proposed in ESP 4 via a new rider.
- Development strategy: planned construction and upgrades to transmission and distribution systems, with capital plans adjusted for financial/economic conditions, load forecasts, legislative/regulatory developments, and environmental standards.

nodes.title: Development Strategy
nodes.heading: Development Strategy —
nodes.start_phrase: Planned construction projects primarily relate to new investments in and upgrades to AES Ohio's transmission and distribution system.
nodes.summary:
- AES Ohio regulatory and market framework:
  - Transmission rates regulated by FERC; formula-based rate effective May 3, 2020; uncontested settlement approved April 15, 2021.
  - Member of PJM RTO, which operates transmission and administers energy, ancillary services, and capacity markets.
  - Ohio SSO rates set through ESP or MRO. In December 2019, PUCO approved AES Ohio’s reversion to ESP 1, reinstating the non-bypassable Rate Stabilization Charge (RSC) with about $79 million in annual revenue. The OCC appealed to the Ohio Supreme Court seeking reversal and potential RSC refunds from August 2021; outcome pending and could be materially adverse.

- ESP 4 filing and distribution rates:
  - ESP 4 filed September 26, 2022: focuses on reliability upgrades, proactive vegetation management, customer programs (renewables, EVs, energy efficiency including low-income), and recovery of certain regulatory assets; excludes continuation of the RSC; PUCO decision anticipated in 2023.
  - Distribution rate case: On December 14, 2022, PUCO approved a $76 million base rate increase, 9.999% ROE, 4.4% long-term debt cost, $783 million rate base, capital structure 53.87% equity/46.13% long-term debt; effective upon approval of a new ESP (expected 2023).

- Smart Grid plan and comprehensive settlement:
  - October 23, 2020 stipulation covering Smart Grid Plan, SEET for 2018–2019, and ESP 1 compliance with SEET and MFA tests.
  - PUCO approved in June 2021; AES contributed $150 million in 2021 for grid modernization. Rehearing applications were denied December 1, 2021; OCC appealed to the Ohio Supreme Court on December 6, 2021; appeal pending.

- Decoupling:
  - January 23, 2020 filing to defer decoupling costs effective December 18, 2019 to mitigate impacts of weather, energy efficiency, and economic demand changes; evidentiary hearing held May 4, 2021; recovery proposed in a new rider within ESP 4.

- AES Ohio capital and development strategy:
  - Planned $1.2 billion capital spend (2023–2025) for transmission and distribution, including Smart Grid Plan.
  - Smart Grid Plan Phase 1: return on and recovery of up to $249 million in investments and related O&M via the Infrastructure Investment Rider over four years, with an aggregate recovery cap of $268 million; AES may file for Phase 2 within three years.
  - Spending contingent on favorable regulatory outcomes.

- AES Clean Energy overview:
  - One of the top U.S. renewables growth platforms with 4,919 MW owned/operated, 2,862 MW under construction (1,707 MW solar, 639 MW wind, 516 MW storage), and a 5.2 GW backlog largely expected online by 2025.
  - IRA expected to accelerate growth; 51 GW U.S. development pipeline.
  - Platform comprises AES Renewable Holdings, sPower, AES Clean Energy Development (ACED), and other assets. ACED formed February 1, 2021 via merger of selected sPower and AES Renewable Holdings projects; expanded with acquisitions of Valcour Intermediate Holdings (wind) and Community Energy (solar).
  - Rapid organizational growth to 1,000+ employees and a more than doubled development pipeline since 2021.
  - February 2023: sold 49% indirect interest in a 1.3 GW operating portfolio (OpCo B: 17 solar, 1 wind across six states) to Hannon Armstrong.

- AES Clean Energy financial drivers:
  - Long-term PPAs underpin revenues; production depends on resource availability and asset performance.
  - Tax credits (ITCs/PTCs) are material; 2022 included $246 million of pre-tax contribution from allocation of tax credits to tax equity partners. Majority of solar financed via tax equity, creating earnings variability due to structure liquidation provisions.
  - IRA extensions and higher credits tied to wage/apprenticeship rules expected to boost demand.

- Market exposure:
  - Laurel Mountain, Buffalo Gap I–III have merchant exposure to PJM and ERCOT price volatility. Laurel Mountain includes 16 MW of battery storage participating in PJM regulation markets.

- Overall strategy:
  - AES Ohio focuses on grid modernization, reliability, targeted customer programs, and regulatory recovery mechanisms.
  - AES Clean Energy targets accelerated U.S. renewables deployment through partnerships, development scale, and tax-efficient financing to meet customer decarbonization goals.

nodes.title: AES Clean Energy

Phase 1 allows return and recovery on up to $249 million of investments and recovery of O&M via the Infrastructure Investment Rider over four years, with a total recoverable cap of $268 million. AES Ohio may file for Phase 2 within three years. Spending depends on favorable regulatory outcomes.

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act is expected to accelerate market growth; AES has a 51 GW development pipeline.

nodes.title: Development Strategy

nodes.start_phrase: As states, communities, and organizations of all types make commitments and plan to reduce their carbon footprints, renewables are the fastest-growing source of electricity generation in the U.S.
nodes.summary:

The approved Phase 1 allows recovery and return on up to $249 million of investments plus O&M through the Infrastructure Investment Rider over four years, with a $268 million aggregate cap on recoverable amounts, and the option to seek Phase 2 approval within three years. - Capital recycling/partnerships: In February 2023, AES sold 49% of its indirect interest in a 1.3 GW operating portfolio (OpCo B; 17 solar, 1 wind across six states) to Hannon Armstrong.

- Key financial drivers: Long-term PPAs underpin revenue; tax incentives (enhanced by the IRA) are significant. In 2022, AES recognized $246 million of pre-tax contribution related to allocation of tax credits to tax equity partners. Many solar assets use tax equity financing, creating earnings variability over time due to structure liquidation provisions. ITC/PTC extensions and bonus credits tied to wage/apprenticeship are expected to boost demand. Certain assets (Laurel Mountain; Buffalo Gap I–III) have merchant exposure to PJM/ERCOT prices; Laurel Mountain includes 16 MW of battery storage participating in PJM regulation markets.

- Development strategy: Co-creating solutions with customers, including 24/7 carbon-free energy for large technology companies. In 2022, 1,990 MW of PPAs were signed/awarded; projects under construction and contracted exceed $6 billion in budget. To address solar supply-chain risks, AES helped form the U.S. Solar Buyer Consortium to support domestic panel manufacturing. The U.S. renewables pipeline expanded to 51 GW in 2022.

- U.S. Conventional Generation: Portfolio operates primarily in CAISO, PJM, and Puerto Rico; AES Southland is the largest asset. The AES Hawaii coal plant PPA expired, and the plant retired in Q3 2022. Many plants provide baseload with availability commitments and potential bonuses; fuel cost dynamics (coal, natural gas, LNG export effects on Henry Hub) impact costs and pricing. PPAs often include fuel cost recovery with profitability influenced by efficiency, availability, heat rate, and fuel flexibility.

- Puerto Rico: AES owns a 524 MW coal-fired cogeneration plant and a 24 MW solar facility (about 8% of the island’s installed capacity), both under long-term PPAs with PREPA expiring in 2027 and 2037. Capacity payments are tied to 12-month rolling availability, with full payment at ≥90% availability. The market features a single grid managed by PREPA, with LUMA operating T&D since June 2021, and oversight by the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau. Puerto Rico’s generation mix is 98% thermal (48% petroleum, 33% natural gas, 17% coal) and 2% renewables. Development strategy aligns with Puerto Rico’s targets of 40% renewables by 2025 and 100% by 2050; AES Clean Flexible Energy is pursuing solar and storage, having executed six contracts on August 26, 2022 for 245 MW of solar PV and 200 MW-4h storage; PREPA launched a second auction on September 28, 2022. - El Salvador: AES is the majority owner of four of five distribution companies (CAESS, CLESA, EEO, DEUSEM), covering 77% of the country and 4,042 GWh of 2022 sales. Generation assets include two AES-owned solar farms (Opico Power 4 MW, Moncagua 3 MW), AES Nejapa biomass (6 MW), and 50% interests in Bosforo (100 MW) and Cuscatlan Solar (10 MW), with output fully contracted to AES utilities. Non-regulated services offered include energy trading, electromechanical construction, O&M, EPC, pole rental, and municipal tax collection.

- El Salvador financial drivers: operational improvements; regulatory outcomes; weather-driven demand variability; and impacts of fuel oil prices on tariffs with a three-month pass-through lag.

- El Salvador regulatory framework and market: Cost-based wholesale market with a marginal economic model under the General Electricity Law. Policy oversight by the National Energy and Hydrocarbons Direction; regulation and tariff-setting by SIGET, with the tariff methodology updated in 2022 for 2023–2027. Distribution rates allow cost recovery and a regulated return on assets. The grid interconnects with Guatemala and Honduras; installed capacity is ~2,250 MW (56% thermal, 25% hydro, 9% solar, 8% biomass, 2% wind).
