nodes.title: Business Description —
nodes.heading: 1.6.2.1 Business Description —
nodes.start_phrase: In Chile, through AES Andes, we are engaged in the generation and supply of electricity (energy and capacity) in the SEN—see Regulatory Framework and Market Structure below.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on AES Andes’ Chilean operations within the SEN (single national power market), highlighting a 3,299 MW installed capacity (excluding storage) and ~11% market share as of December 31, 2022.
- Diversified generation portfolio by geography, technology, and resource, with plants near key demand centers (Santiago, Valparaiso, Antofagasta) to support flexible contracting and operations across hydrological conditions.
- Green Blend strategy to decarbonize and extend PPAs by adding renewables and BESS, committing to no new coal and increased system flexibility and reliability.
- Commercial model centered on long-term PPAs (average remaining term ~10 years) with regulated distributors and unregulated mining/industrial customers; contracts typically include fuel cost pass-through and U.S. CPI indexation.
- Revenue includes energy payments and capacity payments; CEN sets capacity requirements annually, and the National Energy Commission fixes capacity prices semiannually with CPI and other indexation.
- Key financial drivers: spot price dynamics (affected by hydrology, outages, international fuel prices), regulatory cost recovery changes, Chilean peso fluctuations, tax changes, and policies favoring renewables or restricting thermal assets.
- Chile’s market structure: three segments (generation, transmission, distribution) operated by private entities; sales via contracts to regulated/unregulated customers and short-term generator-to-generator trades; prices denominated in USD but paid in CLP.
- SEN overview: 31,141 MW installed (99% of national capacity); CEN dispatches by merit order to minimize system cost while ensuring reliability; regional reliance on thermoelectric generation (especially in the north and during dry conditions).
- 2022 generation mix: 42% thermoelectric, 23% hydro, 20% solar, 13% wind, 2% other; hydrology seasonality (rain Jun–Aug, snowmelt Sep–Dec) materially impacts dispatch and spot prices.
- Oversight by the Ministry of Energy, National Energy Commission, and Superintendency of Electricity and Fuels.
- Customer thresholds: unregulated >5 MW; 0.5–5 MW may choose regime for a minimum four-year term; by law, regulated and unregulated customers contract all electricity needs.
- Chile’s decarbonization plan: retire all SEN coal by 2040 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050; Supreme Decree 42 enables Strategic Reserve Status (SRS) with 60% capacity payments for five years post-shutdown to provide emergency backup.
- Asset transition actions: Ventanas 1 authorized to retire and disconnect from SEN effective June 30, 2022 (previously in SRS); Ventanas 2 shutdown and transition to SRS requested, pending transmission constraints to ensure system stability.

nodes.title: Key Financial Drivers —
nodes.heading: 1.6.2.2 Key Financial Drivers —
nodes.start_phrase: Hedging strategies at AES Andes limit volatility to the underlying financial drivers.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Chile’s electricity market structure and regulation: three segments (generation, transmission, distribution) operated by private companies; single national market (SEN) managed by CEN; oversight by the Ministry of Energy, National Energy Commission, and Superintendency of Electricity and Fuels.
- Explains capacity payments: capacity requirements for each plant; capacity price set semiannually by the National Energy Commission and indexed to CPI and other indices.
- Outlines AES Andes’ key financial drivers and hedging: hedging limits volatility; results influenced by spot prices (affected by hydrology, outages, international fuel), regulatory rulings, Chilean peso fluctuations, tax changes, and policies promoting renewables or restricting thermal plants.
- Details system operations and dispatch: CEN dispatches by merit order to minimize cost while maintaining reliability; thermoelectric plants are critical in south-central SEN during dry conditions and dominate capacity in the northern (Atacama) region; thermoelectric fuels (coal, diesel, LNG) are tied to international prices.
- Provides market size and generation mix: SEN has 31,141 MW (about 99% of national capacity). 2022 mix: 42% thermoelectric, 23% hydro, 20% solar, 13% wind, 2% other.
- Notes hydrology’s impact: rainfall (June–August) and snowmelt (September–December) drive hydro availability, influencing dispatch and spot prices.
- Covers contracting and pricing: generators sell via PPAs to regulated distributors and unregulated customers; unregulated if >5 MW, 0.5–5 MW may choose regime for at least 4 years; energy also tradable bilaterally between generators; prices denominated in USD but paid in Chilean pesos.
- Summarizes decarbonization policy and coal retirements: government targets full coal exit by 2040 and carbon neutrality by 2050; Supreme Decree No. 42 enables Strategic Reserve Status (SRS) with 60% capacity payments for five years post-shutdown to ensure backup availability.
- Reports AES Andes actions: accelerated retirement per government agreement; Ventanas 1 authorized to retire and disconnected effective June 30, 2022 (previously in SRS); shutdown of Ventanas 2 requested, with transition to SRS pending transmission constraints to ensure system stability.

nodes.title: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
nodes.heading: 1.6.2.3 Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
nodes.start_phrase: The Chilean electricity industry is divided into three business segments: generation, transmission, and distribution.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Chilean power market economics: capacity payments set semiannually by the National Energy Commission and indexed; AES Andes uses hedging to limit volatility. Key financial drivers include spot prices (affected by hydrology, outages, international fuels), regulatory changes, FX (Chilean peso), tax policy, and renewable/thermal regulations.
- Market structure and operations: Chile’s single SEN market (31,141 MW; ~99% of national capacity) coordinated by CEN, which dispatches plants by merit order to minimize cost while maintaining reliability. Thermoelectric plants backstop demand, especially in dry years and in the north (Atacama), with fuels (coal, diesel, LNG) tied to international prices. 2022 capacity mix: 42% thermal, 23% hydro, 20% solar, 13% wind, 2% other. Hydrology (rain Jun–Aug; snowmelt Sep–Dec) drives dispatch and spot prices.
- Regulation and contracting: Ministry of Energy, National Energy Commission, and Superintendency oversee the sector. Generators sell via PPAs to regulated distributors or directly to unregulated customers; >5 MW load is unregulated, 0.5–5 MW can opt in/out for at least 4 years. All regulated and unregulated customers must fully contract supply. Electricity priced in USD, paid in CLP; generators can also transact bilaterally outside the spot market.
- Decarbonization policy and coal retirements: National plan to retire all SEN coal by 2040 and reach carbon neutrality by 2050. Decree 42 (2020) enables Strategic Reserve Status (SRS) with 60% capacity payments for five years post-shutdown. AES Andes retired Ventanas 1 (June 30, 2022) and is planning SRS/retirement of Ventanas 2 (expected 2023 SRS; final cessation by Dec 29, 2025). Company committed to enable shutdown of Ventanas 3 & 4 and Angamos 1 & 2 as early as Jan 1, 2025, subject to system conditions. Sold its Guacolda stake (764 MW) in 2021. These actions represent 2.2 GW (72%) of its legacy coal, aligning with the Green Blend transition strategy.
- Environmental obligations: Mandatory NCRE quota met via AES Andes’ solar, wind, and biomass assets. Since 2017, emissions of particulates, SOx, NOx, and CO are taxed; CO2 taxed at $5/ton, with varying PPA pass-through rights. New monitoring for water withdrawals implemented. 2022 brought additional rules: Climate Change Framework Law 21,455; Law 21,505 promoting storage and electromobility; updated operational plans and standards for noise, thermoelectric emissions, industrial effluents, Green Tax offsets, and marine water/sediment quality at Quintero-Puchuncaví.
- Compliance and legal matters: Ongoing environmental sanctioning processes; compliance programs underway for Ventanas and Mesamávida, Cochrane program under review, and Angamos undergoing RCA review (with further details referenced in legal proceedings).
- Growth and transition strategy: Focus on reducing coal intensity and expanding renewables through the Green Blend approach, offering mixes of renewable and nonrenewable solutions to major mining customers. A 4.2 GW development pipeline spans multiple stages and regions, including the contracted Rinconada wind project (258 MW, Biobío) and an expansion of Andes Solar with a co-located battery (186 MW PV + 186 MW, 5-hour storage, Antofagasta).
- Innovation project: The Alba initiative proposes converting Angamos Units 1 and 2 from coal to molten salt thermal storage to deliver emission-free capacity by storing renewable energy as heat for later dispatch.

nodes.title: Environmental Regulation —
nodes.heading: 1.6.2.4 Environmental Regulation —
nodes.start_phrase: Chilean law requires all electricity generators to supply a certain portion of their total contractual obligations with non-conventional renewable energy ("NCRE").
nodes.summary:
- Timelines and coal retirements: Entry into SRS postponed to 2023; definitive shutdown of Ventanas 2 expected by December 29, 2025 (CNE Exempt Resolution No. 555). AES Andes committed to allow shutdown of coal units Ventanas 3, Ventanas 4, Angamos 1 and 2 as early as January 1, 2025, subject to system safety, sufficiency, and competitiveness. In 2021, the Company sold its interest in the 764 MW Guacolda plant. Guacolda, Ventanas, and Angamos total 2.2 GW (72% of AES Andes’ legacy coal fleet). The Green Blend strategy is advancing the phase-out of the remaining coal plants.

- Environmental regulation and compliance: Chile requires generators to meet a portion of contracted supply with non-conventional renewable energy (NCRE); AES Andes complies via its solar, wind, and biomass assets. Since 2017, emissions (particulate matter, SOx, NOx, CO2) are taxed; the CO2 tax is $5/ton, with limited PPA pass-through depending on contract type. From 2021, plants must install water withdrawal monitoring systems; implementation is underway. In 2022, new rules include Law 21,455 (climate change framework), a new Ventanas Operational Plan, emission standards for backup generators, and Law 21,505 promoting energy storage and electromobility. A Prioritized Program of Standards adds obligations on environmental noise, thermoelectric emissions, industrial liquid waste, Green Tax offsets, and marine water/sediment quality for Quintero-Puchuncaví Bay.

- Environmental proceedings: AES Andes and subsidiaries face administrative environmental sanctioning processes. Compliance programs for the Ventanas plant and Mesamávida wind farm are being executed; Cochrane’s program is under authority review. Angamos is under environmental review of its RCA. Related legal matters are referenced in Item 3—Legal Proceedings.

- Development strategy and growth pipeline: The Company aims to reduce coal intensity and expand renewables, supporting major mining customers under the Green Blend approach (mix of renewable and nonrenewable solutions). The development pipeline totals 4.2 GW at various stages and locations. Notable NCRE projects: Rinconada wind (258 MW, Biobío) and an expansion of Andes Solar with co-located storage (186 MW PV + 186 MW, 5-hour battery) in Antofagasta.

- Innovation and conversion initiative: The Alba project, submitted for environmental review by Empresa Eléctrica Angamos, proposes converting Angamos Units 1 and 2 from coal to a molten salt system that stores renewable energy as heat, providing emission-free capacity to the grid.

nodes.title: Development Strategy —
nodes.heading: 1.6.2.5 Development Strategy —
nodes.start_phrase: AES Andes is committed to reducing the coal intensity of the Chilean power grid and plans to increase the renewable energy capacity in its portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- Chile decarbonization and asset transitions:
  - Ventanas 2 operations to cease by December 29, 2025; potential early shutdown (as soon as January 1, 2025, subject to system conditions) of Ventanas 3, Ventanas 4, Angamos 1 and 2 (1,095 MW total).
  - Sale of 100% interest in the 764 MW Guacolda coal plant; together with Ventanas and Angamos, represents 2.2 GW (72%) of AES Andes’ legacy coal fleet transitioned or slated for phase-out.
  - Ongoing “Green Blend” strategy to accelerate remaining coal phase-out and offer mixes of renewable and nonrenewable supply.

- Environmental and regulatory landscape in Chile:
  - NCRE quota compliance met through AES Andes’ solar, wind, and biomass assets.
  - Emissions monitoring/taxation for plants >50 MW (including a $5/ton carbon tax); partial pass-through of green tax costs varies by PPA type.
  - Mandatory water withdrawal monitoring systems being implemented.
  - 2022 regulatory developments: Climate Change Framework Law 21,455; new Ventanas operational plan; backup generator emission standards; Law 21,505 on energy storage and electromobility; prioritized standards on noise, thermoelectric emissions, industrial liquid waste, Green Tax offsets, and marine water/sediment quality in Quintero-Puchuncaví Bay.

- Compliance and legal processes (Chile):
  - Environmental sanctioning processes underway; compliance programs in execution for Ventanas and Mesamávida; Cochrane program under review; Angamos undergoing RCA review. Reference to Form 10-K Item 3—Legal Proceedings.

- Growth and innovation projects (Chile):
  - 4.2 GW development pipeline across stages and geographies.
  - Contracted NCRE projects: Rinconada Wind (258 MW, Biobío) and Andes Solar expansion with 5-hour battery system (186 MW solar + 186 MW storage, Antofagasta).
  - Alba project (Angamos): pioneering conversion of coal units to molten-salt thermal storage providing emission-free capacity.
  - Adelaida green hydrogen pilot: ~1,000 kg/day production (≈2.5 MW).

- Colombia operations and market context:
  - AES Colombia assets: Chivor hydro (1,000 MW), Tunjita run-of-river (20 MW), and solar plants Castilla (21 MW), Brisas (27 MW), San Fernando (61 MW); ~6% of national capacity at end-2022.
  - Business model: contracting with C&I and distribution companies to reduce margin volatility; remainder sold on spot; earns reliability payments for firm energy during scarcity.
  - Key financial drivers: hydrology (dominant), contract coverage, forced outages, COP FX volatility, and spot prices.
  - Market/regulatory framework: Single National Interconnected System (SIN) serves 97% of population; 18,771 MW installed (67% hydro, 3% other renewables, 30% thermal) as of Dec 31, 2022; merit-order dispatch; expansion via reliability charge auctions (conventional) and 15-year contracts for NCRE.
  - Environmental licensing: governed by ANLA under Decree 1076/2015; recent rules on biotic compensation, environmental study guidance, and minor license changes; AES Colombia holds licenses for 406 MW of wind projects.
  - Development strategy: advancing a sizable renewable project pipeline to help customers diversify energy supply and improve competitiveness.

nodes.title: Key Financial Drivers —
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.2 Key Financial Drivers —
nodes.start_phrase: The electricity market in Brazil is highly dependent on hydroelectric generation, therefore electricity pricing is driven by hydrology.
nodes.summary:
- Business strategy: AES Brasil aims to contract most of its physical guarantee and sell the remainder on the spot market; strategy is periodically reassessed and sales are typically via medium-term bilateral contracts. Plant availability and hydrology materially affect exposure to spot prices.
- Ownership and governance: AES increased its economic interest in AES Brasil to 44.1% by end-2020, added another 1.6% in 2021, and migrated AES Brasil to the Novo Mercado (common shares only, higher governance standards). AES maintained majority board representation.
- Capital raises and resulting stakes: 
  - Oct 2021 follow-on: 93 million new shares for $207 million to fund renewables; AES’ indirect interest rose from 45.7% to 46.7%.
  - Sep–Oct 2022 rights offering: 107 million new shares for $197 million; AES Holding Brazil acquired 54 million, lifting AES’ indirect interest to 47.4%.
  - AES Brasil reported within the South America SBU.
- Key financial drivers: hydrology (impacting MRE generation), demand growth, market price risk at re-contracting, asset and cost management, execution of growth strategy, and plant availability.
- Regulatory and market structure in Brazil: 
  - The Ministry of Mines and Energy sets physical guarantees (long-term average producible energy). Energy can be sold via regulated auctions to distributors or unregulated bilateral contracts to large consumers/traders.
  - System overview: 191 GW installed capacity (58% hydro, 25% thermal, 16% other renewables, 1% nuclear). Operations centralized by ONS and regulated by ANEEL; dispatch based on marginal cost and rationing risk considering hydrology, reservoirs, demand, fuel prices, and thermal availability.
  - Hydrology effects: In dry conditions ONS curtails hydro, increases thermal dispatch, raising spot prices; hydro generators may need to buy energy to meet contracts.
  - Risk-sharing: The MRE reallocates hydrological risk using the GSF; deficits require short-term purchases, while surpluses are shared and can be sold on the spot market.

nodes.title: Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.3 Regulatory Framework and Market Structure —
nodes.start_phrase: In Brazil, the Ministry of Mines and Energy determines the maximum amount of energy a generation plant can sell, called physical guarantee, representing the long-term average expected energy production of the plant.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and commercial approach: AES Brasil seeks to contract most of its physical guarantee and sell the balance on the spot market, reassessing its strategy based on market, hydrology, and other factors; typically uses medium-term bilateral contracts.
- Ownership and governance: AES increased its indirect beneficial interest in AES Brasil from 44.1% (end-2020) to 47.4% (Oct 2022) through additional acquisitions and equity offerings. AES Brasil migrated to B3’s Novo Mercado in March 2021, and AES maintained majority board representation. Reported under the South America SBU.
- Capital markets activity: 2021 follow-on offering of 93 million new shares (~$207 million). 2022 private placement of 107 million shares (~$197 million), with AES Holding Brazil subscribing 54 million.
- Key financial drivers: Highly hydrology-dependent Brazilian market; plant availability; demand growth; re-contracting market price risk; asset and cost management; and execution of growth strategy.
- Regulatory and market structure: 
  - Physical guarantee defined by the Ministry of Mines and Energy; sales via regulated auctions or unregulated bilateral contracts.
  - Brazil’s installed capacity ~191 GW: hydro 58%, thermal 25%, renewables 16%, nuclear 1%.
  - ONS centrally dispatches based on marginal cost and rationing risk; unfavorable hydrology raises spot prices and can force hydro plants to buy in the short-term market.
  - MRE/GSF mechanism shares hydrological risk among hydro generators.
  - Law 14.052/2020 set compensation terms for GSF misapplication (2013–2018); ANEEL Resolution 2.919/2021 extended AES Brasil hydro concessions to 2032; terms finalized April 14, 2022.
- Environmental compliance and programs: CONAMA-led licensing; federal/state/municipal inspections. AES Brasil initiatives include producing 1 million native seedlings, reservoir fish repopulation, land fauna conservation, water quality monitoring, and continuous reservoir-edge monitoring via CMR using satellite and field inspections.
- Growth and development strategy: Expand renewable capacity via acquisitions and greenfield builds; prioritize client solutions and innovation; excel in asset management.
- Project pipeline and acquisitions:
  - Cajuína wind complexes (Santa Tereza, São Ricardo, Serra Verde) totaling 1,485 MW greenfield; added Cordilheira dos Ventos components (up to 305 MW) in 2022.
  - Long-term PPAs and 2022 JV investment agreements with BRF (168 MW) and Unipar (91 MW) tied to Cajuína.
  - Sky Arinos solar project (378 MW) acquired March 2022.
  - Operational wind assets acquired Nov 2022: Ventos do Araripe, Caetés, and Cassino (456 MW).
  - São Paulo concession obligation to add 81 MW by Oct 2024; acquired AGV Solar VII (33 MW) in Nov 2021 and continues to pursue remaining capacity.

nodes.title: Environmental Regulation —
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.4 Environmental Regulation —
nodes.start_phrase: In Brazil, the National Environmental Council ("CONAMA") is responsible for environmental licensing procedures.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory developments: Brazil’s Law 14.052/2020 set compensation terms for MRE hydro generators for GSF misapplication (2013–2018), offering concession extensions in exchange for settling reduced GSF payables. ANEEL Resolution 2,919/2021 extended AES Brasil’s hydro concessions from 2029 to 2032; the amended term was finalized on April 14, 2022.
- Environmental compliance and programs: Under CONAMA oversight and multi-level inspections, AES Brasil runs biodiversity and ecosystem programs, including a flora initiative to produce 1 million native seedlings, reservoir fish repopulation, land fauna monitoring and conservation, and water quality monitoring. Reservoir-edge control is conducted by the CMR using change-detection systems, satellite imagery, aerophotogrammetry, and field inspections.
- Strategy: Grow renewable capacity via acquisitions and greenfield projects, enhance client satisfaction and innovation with new energy solutions, and pursue excellence in asset management.
- Portfolio expansion:
  - 2021: Acquisition of the Cajuína wind complexes (Santa Tereza, São Ricardo, Serra Verde) totaling 1,485 MW in Rio Grande do Norte and Ceará.
  - March 2022: Won the process for the Isolated Productive Unit Cordilheira dos Ventos (parts of Facheiro II, Facheiro III, Labocó) in Rio Grande do Norte, adding up to 305 MW to the Cajuína pipeline. Portions of Cajuína are under long-term PPAs; JV investment agreements closed with BRF (168 MW) and Unipar (91 MW).
  - March 2022: Acquisition of Sky Arinos solar project (378 MW) in Arinos, Minas Gerais.
  - November 2022: Acquisition of Ventos do Araripe, Caetés, and Cassino wind complexes (456 MW operational) in Piauí, Pernambuco, and Rio Grande do Sul.
- Concession obligations in São Paulo: Requirement to add 81 MW by October 2024; acquisition of AGV Solar VII (33 MW) on November 30, 2021; ongoing pursuit of remaining capacity.

nodes.title: Development Strategy —
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.5 Development Strategy —
nodes.start_phrase: AES Brasil's strategy is to grow by adding renewable capacity to its generation platform through acquisition or greenfield projects, to focus on client satisfaction and innovation to offer new products and energy solutions, and to be recognized for excellence in asset management.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory update in Brazil: Law 14.052/2020 addressed compensation for MRE hydro generators due to GSF misapplication (2013–2018), offering concession extensions in exchange for settlement of GSF payables; ANEEL Resolution 2.919/2021 extended AES Brasil hydro concessions from 2029 to 2032; amended terms finalized April 14, 2022.

nodes.start_phrase: The following table lists our MCAC SBU generation facilities:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and scale: The MCAC Strategic Business Unit (SBU) operates a 3,390 MW portfolio across three countries (Dominican Republic, Mexico, Panama), spanning gas, pet coke, hydro, wind, solar, and energy storage assets.
- Asset roster by country:
  - Dominican Republic (847 MW, mostly 85% AES-owned): Andres (gas/diesel + 10 MW storage and the country’s only LNG import terminal), Los Mina/DPP (gas + 10 MW storage), Bayasol (50 MW solar), Santanasol (50 MW solar), Agua Clara (50 MW wind). Contracts primarily with Ede Norte, Ede Este, Ede Sur, non-regulated users, with expirations largely in 2023–2039.
  - Mexico (1,361 MW): Merida III (gas/diesel, 505 MW, 75% AES, contracted to CFE to 2025); Mesa La Paz (wind, 306 MW, 50% AES, to 2045 with Fuentes de Energia Peñoles); TEG (pet coke, 275 MW, 99% AES, to 2027 with CEMEX); TEP (pet coke, 275 MW, 99% AES, to 2027 with Peñoles).
  - Panama (1,182 MW): Colon (gas, 381 MW, 100% AES, to 2028) with co-located LNG regasification and storage; multiple hydro plants (Bayano, Chiriqui-Esti, Chiriqui-Los Valles, Chiriqui-La Estrella) at 49% or 90% interests with contracts to 2030; Penonome I (wind, 49%); several 10 MW solar projects (49%); and a 1 MW solar plant serving the Costa Norte LNG Terminal. Customers include ENSA, Edemet, Edechi, and others.
- Contracting and customers: Long-dated PPAs span 2023–2051 with utility and industrial offtakers (e.g., CFE, CEMEX, Peñoles, Dominican distribution companies, and Panamanian distributors).
- Ownership and accounting: Stakes range from 49% to 100%, with certain assets unconsolidated and accounted for as equity affiliates.
- LNG infrastructure: Plants include adjacent regasification facilities and LNG storage tanks (noted capacities of approximately 70–80 TBTU/160,000–180,000 m3). A second LNG storage tank (50 TBTU) in the Dominican Republic is under construction via an equity affiliate, expected online in 1H 2023.
- Projects under construction: Gatun (Panama) gas-fired plant, 670 MW, 49% AES interest, expected commercial operations in 2H 2024.
- AES Dominicana business overview: Five subsidiaries (Andres, Los Mina, Bayasol, Santanasol, Agua Clara) provide 847 MW, representing about 16% of national capacity and ~22% of energy supply. Roughly 668 MW previously contracted through 2022 with government distributors were recontracted in January 2023. AES holds 85% ownership and maintains a strategic partnership with Estrella-Linda. LNG supply: a long-term purchase contract through 1H 2023 (33.6 TBTU/year, Henry Hub–linked) and a new long-term contract through 1H 2025 to support Andres and Los Mina. Andres also holds a long-term contract to sell regasified LNG to industrial users and third-party plants in the country.

nodes.start_phrase: AES Dominicana consists of five operating subsidiaries: Andres, Los Mina, Bayasol, Santanasol and Agua Clara.
nodes.summary:

- Dominican Republic (AES Dominicana):
  - Portfolio: five subsidiaries (Andres, Los Mina, Bayasol, Santanasol, Agua Clara); 847 MW installed; supplies ~16% of national capacity and ~22% of energy demand.
  - Contracting: 668 MW largely contracted through 2022 with distribution companies and large customers; re-contracted with distribution companies in January 2023.

  - Portfolio: five hydro plants (705 MW), a 381 MW gas-fired plant, a 55 MW wind farm, and four 10 MW solar plants (40 MW total), representing ~30% of Panama’s installed capacity.

nodes.title: United States Environmental and Land-Use Legislation and Regulations - Introduction
nodes.source_title: United States Environmental and Land-Use Legislation and Regulations

nodes.heading: 1.10.1 United States Environmental and Land-Use Legislation and Regulations

nodes.summary:
United States Environmental and Land-Use Legislation and Regulations
In the United States, the CAA and various state laws and regulations regulate emissions of SO, NO, particulate matter, GHGs, mercury,
and other hazardous air pollutants. Certain applicable rules are discussed in further detail below.
CSAPR —

nodes.title: CSAPR
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.1 CSAPR —
nodes.start_phrase: CSAPR addresses the "good neighbor" provision of the CAA, which prohibits sources within each state from emitting any air pollutant in an amount which will contribute significantly to any other state’s nonattainment of, or interference with maintenance of, any NAAQS.
nodes.summary:
- The report outlines significant regulatory and environmental compliance risks affecting the company’s global power generation and distribution businesses, including potential impacts from changing laws, remediation obligations (notably coal combustion residuals), enforcement actions, private litigation, and reputational risk.
- It emphasizes stringent and evolving environmental laws worldwide, noting that International Finance Corporation/World Bank-funded projects apply standards often stricter than local laws; the company deploys advanced technologies and controls (e.g., CFB boilers, advanced gas turbines, flue gas desulfurization, and SCR) to mitigate impacts.
- Compliance may require substantial capital and operating expenditures, with uncertainty over the ability to recover costs from customers or counterparties; noncompliance risks include fines, penalties, operational changes, and interruptions.
- The company references ongoing environmental permitting, approvals, and related litigation, directing readers to Legal Proceedings for details.
- U.S. regulatory focus centers on the Clean Air Act and state rules governing SO2, NOx, particulate matter, GHGs, mercury, and other hazardous pollutants.
- Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (CSAPR): The company complies in states including Indiana and Maryland via controls and market-based allowance purchases. The 2016 CSAPR Update and 2021 Revised CSAPR Update (Group 3 trading) reduced ozone-season NOx allowances beginning in 2017 and 2021, potentially requiring additional allowance purchases. A 2022 proposed Federal Implementation Plan tied to the 2015 Ozone NAAQS could further cut allowances as early as 2023. Past costs have been immaterial, but future costs and allowance availability are uncertain and could be material.
- New Source Review (NSR): Ongoing uncertainty over the routine maintenance/replacement exclusion and active EPA enforcement increase risk; an EPA Notice of Violation to AES Indiana is noted. Imposition of NSR requirements could materially adversely impact the business.
- Regional Haze Rule: Future state implementation plans (post-2018 planning periods) may require additional controls to improve visibility in Class I areas by 2064; potential impacts to company facilities remain uncertain.
- National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS): Periodic reviews and tighter standards may drive state plans requiring further emission reductions for ozone, fine particulates, NOx, and SO2, with potentially material compliance costs.
- Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS): The company implemented compliance measures; subsequent legal and policy shifts include a 2015 Supreme Court remand, a 2020 EPA “not appropriate and necessary” determination without removing the source category or changing MATS, court abeyance in 2021, and a 2022 EPA proposal to revoke that determination, signaling potential regulatory adjustments.

nodes.title: New Source Review ("NSR")
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.2 New Source Review ("NSR") —
nodes.start_phrase: The NSR requirements under the CAA impose certain requirements on major emission sources, such as electric generating stations, if changes are made to the sources that result in a significant increase in air emissions.
nodes.summary:
- EPA’s April 6, 2022 proposed Federal Implementation Plan for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS would create a revised CSAPR NOx Ozone Season Group 3 trading program for 25 states (including Indiana and Maryland), likely reducing allowances for EGUs starting in 2023 and potentially requiring additional allowance purchases; future costs are uncertain and could be material, though CSAPR costs to date have been immaterial.
- New Source Review (NSR) under the Clean Air Act: ongoing uncertainty over the routine maintenance, repair, and replacement (RMRR) exclusion and related litigation/enforcement; EPA has issued an NOV to AES Indiana regarding NSR/PSD issues. Imposition of NSR requirements could materially adversely affect the business, financial condition, and results of operations.
- Regional Haze Rule: first planning period had no material impact on AES facilities; states’ second planning period SIPs were due July 31, 2021. No operating states have submitted plans identifying impacts to company facilities yet; future requirements and impacts remain uncertain.
- NAAQS: States must ensure attainment for pollutants including ozone, particulate matter, NOx, and SO2; SIP revisions may impose additional operating limits or emission reductions at generating stations. Compliance costs for U.S. subsidiaries could be material.
- Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS): Rule effective in 2012 and company complied. After a 2015 Supreme Court remand and a 2020 EPA finding that regulation was not “appropriate and necessary” (without delisting the source category or altering MATS), judicial review was held in abeyance; on Feb. 9, 2022, EPA proposed to revoke its prior finding, indicating continued regulatory uncertainty.

nodes.title: Regional Haze Rule
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.3 Regional Haze Rule —
nodes.start_phrase: The EPA's "Regional Haze Rule" established timelines for states to improve visibility in national parks and wilderness areas throughout the United States by establishing reasonable progress goals toward meeting a national goal of natural visibility conditions in Class I areas by the year 2064 through a series of state implementation plans (SIPs), which may result in additional emissions control requirements for electric generating units.
nodes.summary:
- EPA’s April 2022 proposed Federal Implementation Plan for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS would create a revised CSAPR NOx Ozone Season Group 3 program across 25 states (including Indiana and Maryland), likely reducing EGU allowance allocations starting in 2023 and potentially forcing allowance purchases; past costs have been immaterial, but future costs are uncertain and could be material.
- New Source Review (NSR) risk: ongoing uncertainty over the routine maintenance, repair, and replacement (RMRR) exclusion; EPA litigation and Notices of Violation against coal plant owners, including an NOV for AES Indiana; imposition of NSR requirements could materially adversely affect business, financial condition, and results.
- Regional Haze Rule: states must file SIPs to improve visibility toward natural conditions by 2064; first planning period had no material impact on AES facilities; second-period SIPs were due July 31, 2021; no identified impacts to Company facilities to date, but outcomes remain uncertain.
- NAAQS: EPA sets standards for key pollutants (including ozone, particulate matter, NOx, SO2); states may need SIP updates and could require emission reductions or operating limits at Company plants to achieve/maintain attainment; potential compliance costs could be material.
- Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS): rule effective in 2012 and AES complied; 2015 Supreme Court remand for cost consideration; 2020 EPA found regulation not “appropriate and necessary” but retained the source category and MATS requirements; litigation placed in abeyance in 2021; in Feb 2022, EPA proposed to revoke its prior finding (discussion cut off).
- Overall: Significant regulatory and legal uncertainty under the Clean Air Act may lead to additional emissions controls, allowance purchases, operational limits, and potentially material compliance costs for the Company’s U.S. generating fleet.

nodes.title: NAAQS
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.4 NAAQS —
nodes.start_phrase: Under the CAA, the EPA sets NAAQS for six principal pollutants considered harmful to public health and the environment, including ozone, particulate matter, NO, and SO, which result from coal combustion.
nodes.summary:
- EPA proposed a Federal Implementation Plan for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS creating a revised CSAPR NOx Ozone Season Group 3 trading program for 25 states (including Indiana and Maryland), which would reduce EGU allowance allocations starting in 2023 and may necessitate purchasing additional allowances. Past CSAPR compliance costs have been immaterial, but future allowance availability and costs are uncertain and could be material.
- New Source Review (NSR) under the Clean Air Act: ongoing uncertainty over the routine maintenance, repair, and replacement (RMRR) exclusion; EPA enforcement actions and litigation continue, including an NOV to AES Indiana for NSR/PSD issues. Imposition of NSR requirements could have a material adverse impact on the business.
- Regional Haze Rule: states must pursue visibility improvements in Class I areas via SIPs through 2064. First planning period impacts were not material; second-period SIPs were due July 31, 2021. No current state plans identify impacts to company facilities, but outcomes and potential impacts remain uncertain.
- NAAQS: states must ensure attainment/maintenance for pollutants including ozone, particulate matter, NOx, and SO2. States may need SIP revisions that could require emission reductions at company generating stations; related compliance costs could be material.
- Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS): AES facilities implemented compliance measures after the 2012 rule. Following a 2015 Supreme Court remand, the EPA in 2020 found regulation not “appropriate and necessary” but retained the source category and MATS requirements; litigation was held in abeyance. In February 2022, the EPA proposed reversing its 2020 position (proposal text cut off), indicating potential future changes.

nodes.title: Mercury and Air Toxics Standard
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.5 Mercury and Air Toxics Standard —
nodes.start_phrase: In April 2012, the EPA’s rule to establish maximum achievable control technology standards for hazardous air pollutants regulated under the CAA emitted from coal and oil-fired electric utilities, known as “MATS”, became effective and AES facilities implemented measures to comply, as applicable.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on evolving U.S. air quality and climate regulations under the Clean Air Act and their potential material impacts on the company’s coal- and oil-fired generating units, especially in Indiana and Maryland.
- EPA’s proposed 2015 Ozone NAAQS Federal Implementation Plan would revise the CSAPR NOx Ozone Season Group 3 trading program for 25 states, reducing allowances beginning in 2023; past costs immaterial, but future allowance availability and pricing are uncertain and could be material.
- New Source Review: continuing uncertainty over the routine maintenance exclusion and ongoing enforcement; EPA issued a Notice of Violation to AES Indiana. Imposition of NSR requirements could have a material adverse effect.
- Regional Haze Rule: first SIP period caused no material impacts; second-period SIPs were due July 31, 2021. No state plans have identified company impacts to date; future requirements and impacts remain uncertain.
- NAAQS: periodic reviews and potential state SIP revisions could require additional emission reductions for ozone, fine particulate matter, NOx, and SO2; compliance costs could be material.
- Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS): rule remains in effect; legal and regulatory pendulum (2015 Supreme Court remand, 2020 reversal of “appropriate and necessary,” 2022 proposal to reaffirm 2016 finding). Outcomes and cost impacts remain uncertain.
- Greenhouse gases:
  - PSD/BACT permitting could apply to future modifications, potentially adding material compliance costs.
  - NSPS for new/modified units: 2015 CO2 standards premised on partial CCS; 2018 proposal to shift to high-efficiency generation; subsequent rulemakings and challenges are in abeyance.
  - Existing-source rules: ACE Rule replaced the CPP, then was vacated; in 2022 the Supreme Court limited EPA’s Section 111(d) authority regarding generation-shifting. Challenges held in abeyance while EPA develops a replacement rule; impacts could be material. Under ACE, state plans would have covered AES Indiana Petersburg and AES Warrior Run.
- International context: the U.S. rejoined the Paris Agreement in 2021; COP27 announced items such as a loss and damage fund and finance pledges.
- Overall theme: compliance obligations, litigation outcomes, and future rulemakings are uncertain and could materially affect operations, planning, and costs.

nodes.title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.6 Greenhouse Gas Emissions —
nodes.start_phrase: In January 2011, the EPA began regulating GHG emissions from certain stationary sources, including a pre-construction permitting program for certain new construction or major modifications, known as the Prevention of Significant Deterioration ("PSD").
nodes.summary:
- Overview of evolving U.S. environmental regulations affecting the company’s power generation assets, with emphasis on air emissions (MATS, GHG) and water use (cooling water intake/OTC).
- MATS remains in effect; outcomes of ongoing regulatory/judicial processes are uncertain and could affect compliance planning and costs.
- Greenhouse gas regulation status:
  - PSD/BACT could impose GHG controls if future major new sources or major modifications occur; potential compliance costs could be material.
  - NSPS for new/modified/reconstructed electric generating units (2015 CO2 standards) remains in effect; 2018 EPA proposal to revise the standard, and a 2021 EPA rule was vacated by the D.C. Circuit; challenges are on hold.
  - ACE Rule replaced the Clean Power Plan (CPP) in 2019; D.C. Circuit vacated ACE in 2021; U.S. Supreme Court (June 30, 2022) limited EPA’s authority under CAA Section 111(d) by rejecting CPP-style “generation shifting”; D.C. Circuit has held challenges in abeyance while EPA develops a replacement rule.
  - Company highlights uncertainty in future GHG regulations and litigation outcomes; potential impacts could be material, though no current projects are expected to trigger PSD/BACT or NSPS.
  - U.S. rejoined the Paris Agreement (Feb 2021); COP27 developments (e.g., loss and damage fund, climate finance pledges) noted; overall regulatory impacts remain uncertain.
- Cooling Water Intake (CWA Section 316(b)):
  - 2014 EPA rule requires best technology available to reduce fish impingement and, where applicable, entrainment; may necessitate studies and potentially closed-cycle cooling or other technologies.
  - Total impacts and potential capital expenditures are uncertain; costs could be material.
- California Once-Through Cooling (OTC) compliance and fleet transition:
  - AES Southland plans to comply by shutting down and permanently retiring all OTC units at AES Alamitos, AES Huntington Beach, and AES Redondo Beach by SWRCB policy deadlines.
  - Replacement capacity: new air-cooled combined cycle units and battery energy storage at Alamitos and Huntington Beach; 20-year PPAs with Southern California Edison approved by CPUC; construction began in 2017; commercial operation began in early 2020.
  - No plan to replace Redondo Beach OTC units after retirement; some OTC units retired early to free interconnection capacity/emissions credits.
  - SWRCB extended OTC compliance deadlines: Alamitos and Huntington Beach to December 31, 2023; Redondo Beach initially to December 31, 2021, later extended to December 31, 2023 to support grid reliability.
  - Legal challenges to the Redondo Beach extension were largely dismissed, though some related litigation continues; SWRCB decisions reflect reliability considerations informed by SACCWIS recommendations.
- Overall risk statement: Due to regulatory and litigation uncertainty, the company cannot predict precise impacts on operations or financials; potential compliance costs, especially under future Section 111(d) rules or water intake requirements, could be material.

nodes.title: Cooling Water Intake
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.7 Cooling Water Intake —
nodes.start_phrase: The Company's facilities are subject to a variety of rules governing water use and discharge.
nodes.summary:
- Uncertainty around current and future EPA greenhouse gas regulations (BACT and NSPS) and their potential material impact; rules would apply mainly to new or majorly modified sources, and the Company has no such plans currently.
- Cooling Water Intake (CWA Section 316(b)) requirements for reducing fish impingement and entrainment, potential need for closed-cycle cooling, site-specific studies, and potentially material capital expenditures; federal rule upheld by the Second Circuit.
- Compliance with California’s Once-Through Cooling (OTC) Policy: plan to retire OTC units at AES Alamitos, AES Huntington Beach, and AES Redondo Beach; replacement with air‑cooled combined-cycle gas turbines and battery energy storage at Alamitos and Huntington Beach under 20-year PPAs with Southern California Edison; no replacement at Redondo Beach.
- Timeline and regulatory actions on OTC retirements: initial 2020 deadline, extensions for Alamitos and Huntington Beach to December 31, 2023, Redondo Beach to December 31, 2023; litigation by local cities with mixed procedural outcomes; recommendation to extend Alamitos and Huntington Beach to December 31, 2026; draft policy amendment in early 2023, final decision expected in the second half of 2023; NPDES permits administratively extended.
- Statement that California environmental requirements are more stringent and earlier than federal requirements and therefore govern the Company’s California assets.
- Water discharges and jurisdiction: evolving “Waters of the U.S.” (WOTUS) definition—2015 rule, 2019 repeal, 2020 Navigable Waters Protection rule, 2021 nationwide vacatur, and 2023 final rule restoring pre‑2015 framework with updates; pending Supreme Court guidance in Sackett v. EPA; impacts uncertain.
- Effluent Limitation Guidelines (ELG) for steam-electric plants (2015): dry handling of ash and stricter FGD wastewater limits; AES Indiana Petersburg installed dry bottom ash and wastewater treatment; other units use dry handling; potential impacts from litigation or revisions uncertain.
- Maui “functional equivalent” Supreme Court decision potentially expanding permit requirements for discharges via groundwater; ongoing litigation creates uncertainty about impacts.
- Selenium aquatic life criterion (2016): possible NPDES permit updates and site-specific evaluations; total impacts not yet predictable.

nodes.title: Water Discharges
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.8 Water Discharges —
nodes.start_phrase: In June 2015, the EPA and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers ("the agencies") published a rule defining federal jurisdiction over waters of the U.S., known as the "Waters of the U.S." (WOTUS) rule.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Clean Water Act (CWA) compliance issues affecting AES’s U.S. power plants, highlighting California’s more stringent requirements and earlier compliance timelines compared to federal rules.
- California OTC/316(b) compliance: SWRCB consideration of extending OTC compliance dates for AES Huntington Beach and AES Alamitos to December 31, 2026; draft OTC Policy amendment released early 2023; final decision expected in the second half of 2023. Federal EPA 316(b) rule upheld by the Second Circuit in 2018; compliance costs could be materially impactful.
- Evolving federal jurisdiction over “Waters of the U.S.” (WOTUS): regulatory shifts from the 2015 rule to the 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule, its 2021 nationwide vacatur, and a January 2023 final rule restoring pre-2015 definitions with updates; related Supreme Court litigation (Sackett v. EPA) could clarify wetland jurisdiction tests; impacts remain uncertain.
- Effluent Limitation Guidelines (ELG) for steam-electric power plants: requirements for dry handling of fly and bottom ash and stricter limits for flue gas desulfurization wastewater; AES Indiana Petersburg has installed compliant systems; other U.S. operations largely already use dry handling; potential material impacts undetermined pending litigation and revisions.
- Groundwater discharge permitting: 2020 Supreme Court decision (County of Maui) establishing that “functional equivalent” discharges to navigable waters via groundwater may require NPDES permits; ongoing litigation creates uncertainty around impacts.
- Selenium water quality criteria (2016): possible NPDES permit updates with site-specific effluent limits; overall impacts not yet predictable.

nodes.title: Selenium Rule
nodes.heading: 1.10.1.9 Selenium Rule —
nodes.start_phrase: In June 2016, the EPA published the final national chronic aquatic life criterion for the pollutant selenium in fresh water.
nodes.summary:
- Cooling Water Intake Structures/CWA 316(b): California OTC policy extension under consideration to December 31, 2026 for AES Huntington Beach and AES Alamitos; state rules currently more stringent than federal; Second Circuit upheld federal rule; compliance costs could be material.
- Water discharges (WOTUS): Ongoing shifts in the federal definition of “waters of the U.S.” (2015 rule, 2019 repeal, 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule, 2021 vacatur, 2023 final rule restoring pre-2015 framework with updates); Supreme Court review in Sackett v. EPA on wetlands test; impacts uncertain.

nodes.title: Risks Associated with our Operations
nodes.heading: 2.1 Risks Associated with our Operations
nodes.start_phrase: The operation of power generation, distribution and transmission facilities involves significant risks.
nodes.summary: The excerpt is from Item 1A—Risk Factors of a 2022 Annual Report, introducing overall risk categories (operations, regulation/laws, indebtedness/financial condition) and then detailing operational risks for a power generation and distribution company. It highlights potential reductions in facility availability due to outages, equipment or transmission failures, labor disputes, fuel supply disruptions, adverse hydrologic/wind conditions, regulatory or permitting issues, and catastrophic events (natural disasters, dam failures, explosions, terrorism, vandalism, cyber-attacks). It warns of rising operating costs for fuel and transport, purchased power, operations and maintenance, repairs, environmental compliance (including emissions offsets and capital for controls), transmission access, and insurance. The business depends on reliable transportation, power, and water infrastructure; interruptions or third-party disruptions can impede production, while aging plants and supply-chain constraints (especially with limited suppliers) may require significant capital and risk downtime; failures may trigger penalties, liquidated damages, or termination under power purchase agreements. It underscores inherent hazards of power operations (fuel handling, rotating equipment, electricity delivery) from natural events and operational failures, noting that training, procedures, maintenance, and quality controls may not fully prevent losses. It also calls out specific lithium-ion battery storage risks, including rare thermal runaway events that can ignite nearby materials despite newer design mitigations. Overall, occurrence of these risks could materially and adversely affect business, financial results, and condition.

structure.title: RISK F ACTORS
structure.heading: ITEM 1A. RISK F ACTORS
structure.start_phrase: You should consider carefully the following risks, along with the other information contained in or incorporated by reference in this Form 10- K.
structure.summary:
- The excerpt is from Item 1A—Risk Factors of a 2022 Annual Report, outlining risks tied to operations, governmental regulation and laws, and indebtedness/financial condition, with cross-references to MD&A and financial statements.
- Operational risks:
  - Power generation, transmission, and distribution hazards (outages, equipment failures, fuel disruptions, regulatory noncompliance, natural disasters, terrorism, cyberattacks, labor disputes).
  - Aging infrastructure requiring significant maintenance; supply-chain constraints and single/limited-source suppliers; potential inability to obtain critical parts.
  - Battery storage risks specific to lithium-ion thermal events.
  - Safety incidents can lead to injury, environmental damage, business interruption, litigation, fines, and penalties.
  - Ongoing material litigation and regulatory proceedings may have adverse outcomes.
- International exposure:
  - Significant operations in developing countries with risks including political/economic instability, FX volatility, repatriation limits, legal/regulatory unpredictability, expropriation, permit delays, tax changes, contract enforceability issues, and FCPA/anti-bribery compliance; higher financing risk relying on multilaterals/government guarantees; revenue/margin volatility.
- Market and commodity risks:
  - Exposure to wholesale electricity spot market price volatility for sales and purchases; multiple drivers of volatility (fuel prices, transmission constraints, renewables penetration, distributed generation, weather, regulation, economic conditions).
  - Increasing price volatility and declining PPA prices due to low-cost renewables and cheap natural gas may pressure existing assets and future growth opportunities.
  - Adverse developments in China’s economy could reduce commodity demand and electricity demand in key markets.
  - Insurance coverage may be inadequate or unavailable, especially for coal and hydro; reliance on a captive insurer (AGIC).
- Contracting and counterparty risks:
  - Reliance on long-term PPAs and fuel supply agreements; inability to renew or secure new long-term contracts may force merchant exposure; counterparty credit risk (including sub-investment-grade offtakers) and potential PPA rejection in bankruptcy.
  - Supplier/customer concentration increases credit and performance risk; potential breaches and cascading defaults.
- Renewables and development risks:
  - Dependence on regulatory incentives (ITC/PTC, RPS, RECs, tax exemptions) and permitting; uncertainty around future availability and usage of incentives.
  - U.S. Department of Commerce AD/CVD circumvention investigation on Southeast Asian solar supply chains could impose tariffs, impairing U.S. renewables strategy and project returns.
  - Resource variability (wind/solar) impacts production; merchant exposure where long-term contracts are unavailable; capital intensity and financing constraints; schedule delays can defer tax credits and revenue.
  - Development risks: siting, financing, engineering/construction, interconnection/transmission, supply-chain disruptions, commissioning delays, community opposition; potential obligations before securing financing/PPAs/permits; risk of project abandonment and write-offs.
  - Acquisition risks: integration challenges, returns below expectations, unforeseen liabilities, and complexities transitioning previously state-owned or integrated utilities.
- Pandemic risk:
  - COVID-19 impacts on demand, customer payment behavior, regulatory moratoria, force majeure claims, spot prices, workforce health, fuel logistics, maintenance, supply chain, cybersecurity, project delays, capital markets access, asset sales, FX/commodity volatility, impairments, and regulatory recoveries; could exacerbate other risks.
- Competitive and technology risks:
  - Intensifying competition for PPAs and asset acquisitions; disruptive technologies and non-traditional entrants; potential margin compression.
  - Technological change (distributed generation, storage, advances in solar/wind/alternative fuels) may require significant capex or render assets obsolete.
- Cybersecurity and data privacy:
  - Threats to operational and enterprise IT systems; potential operational, financial, legal, and reputational impacts despite mitigation; heightened geopolitical risk.
  - Increasing global data privacy obligations and exposure to penalties and claims from breaches, including through equity affiliates.
- Weather, hydrology, and natural disasters:
  - Demand and generation variability due to abnormal weather; wind/solar resource uncertainty; hydrology-driven volatility and costly spot purchases in drought (e.g., Panama 2019, Brazil 2021).
  - Severe weather/natural disasters (hurricanes, floods, earthquakes, etc.) and climate change intensification increase outage, safety, environmental, and repair/recovery cost risks; regulatory uncertainty over cost recovery.
- Joint ventures/equity investments:
  - Limited control and dependency on partners; approval rights may restrict distributions or transfers; partner insolvency risks; potential misalignment with Fluence’s board; Fluence material weakness in internal controls affecting reliability of reported results.
- Financial market and hedging risks:
  - FX translation and transaction exposures; commodity and interest-rate hedging may be incomplete or ineffective; basis risk, counterparty default, and accounting volatility.
- Utility-specific risks:
  - Slower customer growth or usage due to efficiency and economic/demographic trends may undermine returns on investment.
- Pension and asset impairment:
  - Defined benefit plan exposure to market/assumption changes requiring higher contributions.
  - Triggers for impairment of long-lived assets (market, regulatory, cost, contract losses) could materially affect results and net worth.
- Regulatory and environmental risks:
  - Broad regulatory exposure: tariffs/rate of return determinations, recoverability of costs, tax changes, contract enforceability, environmental constraints, licensing/permitting, derivatives reporting/clearing rules (e.g., EMIR).
  - Coal Combustion Residuals (CCR) liabilities and enforcement by EPA/states/private parties; remediation costs, lawsuits, and reputational risk.
  - FERC/NERC/state utility commission oversight: competition policies, demand response, transmission expansion, PURPA obligation waivers, and significant civil/criminal penalties for violations; extensive state regulation in Indiana/Ohio.
  - Environmental compliance under air, water, waste, endangered species laws; NSR/PSD enforcement actions and costly controls or accelerated retirements; uncertainty of recovering environmental costs.
  - GHG/climate risks: substantial CO2 emissions; evolving U.S. regulatory landscape (NSPS, ACE Rule litigation, Supreme Court limits on generation shifting, potential future Section 111(d) rules), Paris Agreement pressures, decarbonization initiatives (e.g., Chile, Hawaii, Puerto Rico) potentially accelerating coal retirements, impairments, and recovery risks; physical climate impacts on operations; reputational and litigation exposure.
- Tax policy:
  - U.S. Inflation Reduction Act benefits for clean energy (extended/enhanced credits) and a 15% corporate alternative minimum tax; ongoing evaluation of impacts.
  - EU Pillar 2 15% global minimum tax adoption; potential material effects pending national transposition.
- Indebtedness, liquidity, and capital access:
  - High consolidated debt (~$23 billion), largely secured at subsidiaries; constraints on flexibility, increased vulnerability to market conditions, refinancing risk, and potential for more onerous covenants.
  - Parent is a holding company reliant on subsidiary distributions subject to debt covenants, local rules, and repatriation limits.
  - Some subsidiaries in default on debts (non-recourse), potentially reducing upstream cash, triggering parent guarantees or broader defaults, and risking foreclosure/write-downs.
  - Significant parent cash needs (debt service, dividends, capex, acquisitions, buybacks, taxes) funded by subsidiary distributions, parent financings, and asset sales; availability uncertain.
  - Dependence on capital markets and tax equity; credit rating downgrades could raise costs, reduce access, and require collateral; common stock price volatility risk.
- Other items:
  - No unresolved SEC staff comments (Item 1B).
  - Properties primarily leased and commonly encumbered by project financings (Item 2).
  - Legal proceedings: routine litigation with reserves believed adequate; specific long-running arbitration in India (GRIDCO) alleging obligations under a comfort letter and seeking significant damages (Item 3).

- Item 3—Legal Proceedings: the company faces routine claims and has recorded reserves where losses are probable and estimable; believes outcomes are unlikely to be materially adverse, though unfavorable results could be material. Specific matter: a long-standing arbitration initiated in December 2001 by Grid Corporation of Odisha (GRIDCO) against the company, AES Orissa Distribution Private Limited, and Jyoti Structures regarding a shareholders agreement tied to CESCO; GRIDCO alleges a company comfort letter requires additional financial support for CESCO’s obligations to GRIDCO and seeks approximately $189 million in damages (plus unspecified amounts).

  - Item 2 (Properties): Global offices primarily leased; most generation facilities subject to project finance liens and located on leased land, with some unencumbered owned interests.
  - Item 4 (Mine Safety): Not applicable.

- Legal proceedings overview
  - Company accrues when loss is probable and estimable; believes current matters are unlikely to be materially adverse overall, but some outcomes could be material and are not presently estimable.

- Key legal and regulatory matters by jurisdiction
  - India: GRIDCO arbitration (Odisha). 2007 award rejected GRIDCO’s claims; costs awarded to respondents. GRIDCO’s challenge to liability award still pending; company maintains defenses.
  - Brazil: Creosote contamination at former pole factory (AES Sul/AES Florestal). Public civil action seeking mitigation and indemnity (~R$6m); estimated remediation R$15–60m. AES Sul sold in 2016; potential liability retained by AES Guaiba; defenses asserted.
  - United States – California: AES Redondo Beach wetlands dispute with California Coastal Commission. Site sold in 2020 with purchaser assuming obligations; NOV requires Coastal Development Permit for pump removal/operations; CDP under City review.
  - United States – Indiana: Clean Air Act NOVs at Petersburg Station. 2021 consent decree: stricter emissions limits and caps, $1.5m civil penalty, $5m non-emitting generation project, $0.3m state environmental project; Units 1 and 2 retired by July 1, 2023 or install SNCR on Unit 4.
  - Chile (AES Andes):
    - Coal waste on Ventanas beach: fine imposed (~$341k) under continued administrative appeal.
    - Ventanas Complex SMA sanctions: Compliance Program approved; additional emissions-offset actions required (street paving or community heaters); Program cost ~$10.8m; fines possible for unsatisfactory execution.
    - Mesamávida wind project: SMA charges; Compliance Program (~$4.3m) approved; third-party court challenge pending; fines possible if challenge succeeds or execution unsatisfactory.
    - Cochrane Power Station: SMA sanctioning on four charges (one “serious”); Compliance Program submitted (~$340k); fines possible if not approved/executed satisfactorily.
    - Alto Maipo SpA: Four “serious” SMA charges (construction/environmental noncompliance); considering a Compliance Program; potential outcomes include fines, permit revocation, or closure.
  - Dominican Republic: Multiple civil lawsuits (2018, 2019, 2022) against AES entities alleging personal injury/death from CCRs delivered in 2003–2004; damages sought approx. $476m, >$900m, and >$600m; claims lack individualized injury detail; AES contesting.
  - Mexico:
    - CFE arbitration (AES Mérida III): CFE sought ~$200m in refunds and ~$480m in damages; November 2022 tribunal rejected CFE’s damages and awarded AES Mérida a net amount on counterclaims; CFE compliance/challenge uncertain.
    - Environmental audits at TEG/TEP: TEG fined ~MXN 8.47m (~USD $0.4m) for alleged air/reporting breaches; nullity action and provisional injunction in place; related bail challenge via amparo. TEP filed amparo over agency inaction; audit resolution pending.
  - Puerto Rico: EPA NOV to AES Puerto Rico alleging MATS and Title V noncompliance (emission exceedances, monitoring, reporting); discussions ongoing; potential for civil penalties and remedial measures.

structure.title: Executive Summary
structure.heading: Executive Summary
structure.start_phrase: In 2022, AES delivered on its strategic and financial objectives.
structure.summary:
- Context: Item 7 MD&A excerpt from AES’s 2022 Annual Report, covering the Executive Summary and a review of consolidated results of operations with segment detail and definitions of key terms.
- Strategic execution: Completed or acquired 1.9 GW of renewables and energy storage; signed long‑term PPAs for an additional 5.2 GW.
- GAAP earnings: Diluted loss per share from continuing operations increased from $0.62 to $0.82, driven by the absence of prior‑year gains (sPower remeasurement and Fluence capital raise), higher income tax expense, lower US & Utilities contributions (recognition of deferred power purchase costs and outages), prior‑year realized gains on de‑designated interest rate swaps at the Parent, higher interest expense, and lower capitalized interest in Chile; partially offset by the absence of the prior‑year Alto Maipo deconsolidation loss and stronger MCAC LNG margins.
- Non‑GAAP performance: Adjusted EPS rose from $1.52 to $1.67, led by higher MCAC contributions (favorable LNG) and South America (higher margins and increased ownership in AES Andes), partially offset by lower US & Utilities contributions, the absence of prior‑year swap gains, and higher interest expense.
- Revenue: Total up 13% to $12.6B. By SBU: US & Utilities +16%, South America flat, MCAC +33%, Eurasia +8%; Corporate & Other modest; Eliminations slightly higher.
- Operating margin: Total down 6% to $2.55B. By SBU: US & Utilities −29%, South America −23%, MCAC +57%, Eurasia +9%; Corporate & Other +11%; Eliminations increased.
- Notable P&L items: G&A +25%; interest expense +23% (interest income +31%); goodwill impairment of $777M; asset impairments of $763M (lower than 2021); other income sharply lower versus prior year; foreign currency losses; income tax shifted to expense from prior‑year benefit.
- Bottom line: Loss from continuing operations improved to $(505)M from $(955)M, but net loss attributable to AES widened to $(546)M from $(409)M due to changes in noncontrolling interests.
- Cash flow: Net cash provided by operating activities increased 43% to $2.72B.
- Definitions: Clarifies components of revenue (regulated utilities and non‑regulated generation, derivative gains/losses), cost of sales (fuel/electricity purchases, O&M, D&A, bad debt, direct support costs, derivative gains/losses), and operating margin (revenue less cost of sales).

structure.title: Review of Consolidated Results of Operations
structure.heading: Review of Consolidated Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
Revenue includes revenue earned from the sale of energy from our
utilities and the production and sale of energy from our generation plants, which are classified as regulated and non-regulated, respectively, on
