structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: Excerpt from AES Corporation’s 2022 Annual Report reviewing consolidated results of operations for 2022, 2021, and 2020. Presents revenue and operating margin by SBU (US & Utilities; South America; MCAC; Eurasia), corporate/eliminations, and key non-operating items. Defines revenue, cost of sales, and operating margin.

- Headline results:
  - Total revenue rose 13% to $12.6B in 2022 (2021: +15% to $11.1B).
  - Total operating margin fell 6% to $2.55B in 2022 (2021: +1% to $2.71B).
  - Net loss from continuing operations improved to $(505)M in 2022 from $(955)M in 2021.
  - Net loss attributable to AES widened to $(546)M in 2022 from $(409)M in 2021.
  - Operating cash flow increased to $2.72B in 2022 from $1.90B in 2021.

- Revenue drivers:
  - 2022 vs. 2021: Growth led by MCAC (LNG transactions; higher contract/spot sales on better hydrology and demand; Mexico pass-through fuel) and US & Utilities (rider increases at AES Indiana/Ohio; demand/weather; AES Clean Energy growth incl. Google supply agreement and new projects; Southland spot; El Salvador pass-through). Eurasia benefited from higher prices/generation (Bulgaria), St. Nikola prices, and Mong Duong construction revenue. Offsets included Itabo sale and AES Hawaii plant closure; higher unrealized derivative losses at Southland.
  - 2021 vs. 2020: Broad-based increases at US & Utilities (Southland Energy PPAs active all year; El Salvador recovery; AES Indiana fuel/demand; hedging gains; AES Clean Energy/Google), MCAC (DR contracts/fuel/LNG; Mexico pass-through; Panama prices/demand; offset Itabo sale), South America (Angamos contract termination revenue; Argentina prices/generation; Colombia hydrology; AES Brasil acquisitions; FX headwinds), and Eurasia (Bulgaria/Vietnam generation and prices).

- Operating margin drivers:
  - 2022 decline: Lower margins in South America (absence of Angamos termination revenue; Argentina regulatory receivable allowances; higher purchases/fixed costs at AES Brasil; FX) and US & Utilities (unrealized derivative losses at Southland Energy; regulatory items at AES Indiana/Ohio; AES Hawaii closure; AES Puerto Rico outages/heat rate; higher growth costs at AES Clean Energy). Partly offset by stronger MCAC (LNG, hydrology, higher prices/demand) and modest gains in Eurasia.
  - 2021 slight increase: Gains in US & Utilities (Southland Energy PPAs; hedging; El Salvador demand), Corporate/Other allocations and self-insurance, and Eurasia; offset by declines in South America (FX; drier hydrology; spot prices; Chile prior-period effects; partly offset by Angamos termination revenue, Argentina prices, Colombia hydrology) and MCAC (Itabo sale; DR capacity; Mexico availability/costs; Panama hydrology; partly offset by DR LNG and Panama renewables).

- Expense and other income items:
  - G&A: Up 25% in 2022 on development and people costs; flat in 2021 vs. 2020.
  - Interest expense: Up 23% in 2022 (absence of prior swap gains, lower capitalized interest, higher borrowings); down 12% in 2021 (swap gains, Parent refinancing, Brazil GSF effect).
  - Interest income: Up 31% in 2022 (short-term investments AES Brasil/Argentina; higher CAMMESA rates; Alamitos STL growth); up 11% in 2021 (Chile arbitration; Alamitos STL; CAMMESA).
  - Loss on extinguishment of debt: Down sharply in 2022; lower again from 2020 to 2021; with entity-specific refinancings noted.
  - Other income: Down materially in 2022 due to absence of 2021 gains (sPower remeasurement on AES Clean Energy merger, Alto Maipo arbitration, contingent consideration at AES Clean Energy); partially offset by 5B remeasurement gain and insurance proceeds. Large increase in 2021 vs. 2020.
  - Other expense: Slightly higher in 2022 (AES Gilbert disposition/lease allowance); higher in 2021 on lease commencement loss and other disposals.

- Disposals and impairments:
  - Loss on disposal/sale of business interests: Minimal in 2022 vs. large 2021 loss from Alto Maipo deconsolidation; 2021 also included Fluence-related gain.
  - Goodwill impairment: $777M in 2022 (AES Andes $644M; AES El Salvador $133M) due to higher discount rates/country risk; none in 2021/2020.
  - Asset impairments: $763M in 2022 (Maritza coal plant Bulgaria; TEG TEP Mexico; Amman East/IP4 Jordan), down from $1.575B in 2021 (AES Andes coal retirements; Puerto Rico coal ash costs; Buffalo Gap wind; Mountain View wind). 2020 included Angamos/Ventanas and Hawaii impairments.
  - Other non-operating expense: $175M in 2022 for other-than-temporary impairment of sPower equity method investment (HLBV effects; OpCo B sale closed Feb 2023); $202M in 2020 for OPGC impairment and sale; none in 2021.

- Foreign currency:
  - Net transaction losses of $77M in 2022 (mainly Argentina peso depreciation; partly offset by Colombian FX derivative gains); $10M loss in 2021; $55M gains in 2020. Country detail provided.

- Income taxes:
  - 2022 expense $265M; effective rate (157)%, driven by nondeductible goodwill impairments (Andes/El Salvador) and Maritza impairment; partially offset by MCAC LNG and Argentina inflation/FX effects.
  - 2021 benefit $133M; effective rate 13%, influenced by Alto Maipo deconsolidation, Puerto Rico impairment, US 2017 tax exam closure, and Brazilian valuation allowance release.
  - 2020 expense $216M; effective rate 44%, impacted by OPGC impairment and Uruguaiana sale; partially offset by ITC for Na Pua Makani.

- Affiliates and noncontrolling interests:
  - Net equity in losses of affiliates rose to $71M in 2022 (lower sPower earnings; higher Fluence losses); fell sharply in 2021 vs. 2020 (sPower turned to earnings; fewer AES Andes losses; offset by higher Fluence/Uplight losses).
  - NCI/redeemable interests swung from $(542)M in 2021 to $41M income in 2022, reflecting prior-year Alto Maipo deconsolidation loss, Buffalo Gap impairments, lower tax equity loss allocations; offset by higher Clean Energy development costs, ownership changes at AES Andes, prior Brazil tax benefits, and Jordan impairments.

- Bottom line bridge:
  - 2022 vs. 2021: Larger AES net loss due to goodwill impairments, absence of Fluence IPO and sPower remeasurement gains, higher taxes and Parent interest, lower US & Utilities margins, lower capitalized interest, and sPower impairment; partially offset by no Alto Maipo deconsolidation loss, lower long-lived asset impairments, and stronger MCAC margins.
  - 2021 vs. 2020: Shift to net loss driven by Alto Maipo deconsolidation loss, higher asset impairments, and lower South America margins; partly offset by Fluence IPO gain, sPower remeasurement gain, lower Parent interest and extinguishment losses, stronger US & Utilities margins, and lower taxes.

- Segments and non-GAAP:
  - SBUs cover US & Utilities (US, Puerto Rico, El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe, Asia).
  - Non-GAAP measures used: Adjusted Operating Margin, Adjusted PTC, Adjusted EPS. Definitions updated in 2021 to remove restructuring-cost adjustments and include a US tax exam benefit; 2020 definitions exclude Angamos early termination gains to improve comparability.

structure.title: SBU Performance Analysis
structure.heading: SBU Performance Analysis
structure.start_phrase:
We are organized into four market-oriented SBUs: US and Utilities (United States, Puerto Rico, and El Salvador); South America (Chile,
Colombia, Argentina, and Brazil); MCAC (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean); and Eurasia (Europe and Asia).
structure.summary:
- Explains year-over-year changes in net income attributable to The AES Corporation, highlighting a 2021 loss versus 2020 income, driven by the deconsolidation loss at Alto Maipo (post-Chapter 11), higher impairments, and weaker South America margins (Brazil GSF), partially offset by gains from Fluence’s IPO, sPower remeasurement, lower Parent interest expense, and improved US and Utilities margins with lower tax expense.
- Outlines AES’ four market-oriented SBUs: US and Utilities; South America; MCAC (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean); and Eurasia.
- Details non-GAAP measures used by management and investors—Adjusted Operating Margin, Adjusted PTC, and Adjusted EPS—including:
  - Rationale for use and GAAP comparables.
  - Definition updates: 2021 inclusion of tax exam UTP reversal under U.S. tax reform item; removal (effective 1/1/2021) of restructuring-program adjustment; 2020 exclusion of Angamos early termination gains for comparability.
  - Core exclusions: unrealized derivative/equity securities gains/losses, unrealized FX, disposition/acquisition impacts (including early closures and certain lease accounting), impairments, early debt retirement, and Angamos termination gains; HLBV allocations to NCI are not adjusted.
- Presents reconciliations:
  - Adjusted Operating Margin: $2,153m (2022), $1,721m (2021), $1,728m (2020), reconciling for NCI, unrealized derivatives, disposition/acquisition effects, and Angamos gains.
  - Adjusted PTC: $1,567m (2022), $1,418m (2021), $1,247m (2020), adjusting for unrealized derivatives/equities, FX, dispositions/acquisitions, impairments, debt extinguishment, and Angamos gains.
  - Adjusted EPS: $1.67 (2022), $1.52 (2021), $1.44 (2020); includes treatment of dilutive securities when GAAP EPS is a loss and itemized adjustments.
- Summarizes notable items affecting Adjusted EPS across periods: significant impairments (e.g., AES Andes, AES El Salvador, Maritza, TEG TEP, Puerto Rico), Alto Maipo deconsolidation loss, gains from Fluence IPO/share issuance and sPower remeasurement, divestitures (e.g., Guacolda, OPGC, Uruguaiana, Kazakhstan HPPs), various debt extinguishment losses, and related tax impacts (including 2021 U.S. tax exam closure).
- SBU performance analysis with 2022 vs. 2021 and 2021 vs. 2020 drivers:
  - US and Utilities: 2022 Operating Margin declined due to Southland Energy unrealized derivative losses and outages, AES Ohio cost recognition, AES Hawaii outages/closure, Puerto Rico forced outages/maintenance, AES Indiana settlement and higher maintenance; partially offset by new project revenue and Google 24/7 CFE contract; 2021 improvement from Southland PPAs and hedging, and El Salvador demand recovery. Adjusted PTC followed these trends, also reflecting development costs and timing of renewables CODs.
  - South America: 2022 GAAP down on absence of Angamos termination gains; Adjusted results up on increased ownership in AES Andes to 99%, stronger Chile contract margin and lower coal depreciation, better Brazil hydrology, and higher Colombia spot margins; 2021 declines tied to Brazil’s prior-year GSF settlement and other country-specific factors; Adjusted PTC impacted by interest, FX in Argentina, and arbitration outcomes.
  - MCAC: 2022 strong gains from favorable LNG transactions and pricing in Panama and the Dominican Republic; 2021 comparisons reflect Itabo sale and mixed operational trends; Adjusted PTC improved significantly in 2022, partially offset by higher post-buyout interest allocation at Colón.
  - Eurasia: Modest 2022 increase from Mong Duong construction revenue and Bulgaria merchant prices; 2021 gains from higher prices and generation; 2022 Adjusted PTC slightly lower due to higher interest expense.
- Notes ownership changes affecting results: increased stakes in AES Brasil (2020) and AES Andes from 67% to 99% in early 2022.
- Concludes with key trends and uncertainties: operational and supply-chain risks, including U.S. trade actions on Southeast Asian solar imports and a 24-month tariff waiver issued June 6, 2022; acknowledges potential material impacts from FX/commodity volatility absent offsets from operating improvements, growth, and cost reductions.

structure.title: Key Trends and Uncertainties
structure.heading: Key Trends and Uncertainties
structure.start_phrase: During 2023 and beyond, we expect to face the following challenges at certain of our businesses.
structure.summary:
- Eurasia SBU performance summary with Operating Margin, Adjusted Operating Margin, and Adjusted PTC (non-GAAP, adjusted for NCI) for 2022, 2021, and 2020, including year-over-year changes.
- 2022 vs. 2021 drivers:
  - Operating Margin up $20 million (9%): +$15 million from Mong Duong construction revenue (lower expected completion costs for ash pond 2, offset by higher maintenance); +$11 million from higher merchant prices at St. Nikola (partly offset by Euro depreciation); other -$6 million.
  - Adjusted Operating Margin up $10 million reflecting the above, adjusted for NCI.
  - Adjusted PTC down $4 million due to higher interest expense, partly offset by higher Adjusted Operating Margin.
- 2021 vs. 2020 drivers:
  - Operating Margin up $30 million (16%): +$19 million from higher electricity prices and generation at Maritza and St. Nikola; +$4 million improved performance at Mong Duong; +$7 million other.
  - Adjusted Operating Margin up $20 million; Adjusted PTC up $19 million.
- Key trends and uncertainties:
  - Trade restrictions and solar supply chain: U.S. Commerce circumvention investigation on Southeast Asia solar imports; Presidential 24‑month tariff waiver; Dec. 2, 2022 preliminary affirmative findings of circumvention with company-specific outcomes; UFLPA import impacts; AES secured 2023 U.S. panel needs; ongoing uncertainty.
  - COVID-19: Essential operations maintained; revenue stability supported by regulated/long-term contracts; 2022 performance consistent with recovery.
  - Estí hydro (Panama): September 30, 2022 flooding; plant offline for repairs; business interruption/property insurance in place with partial settlement; carrying value $130 million deemed recoverable.
  - Macroeconomic/political changes and FX volatility may affect taxes and energy policy.
  - U.S. Inflation Reduction Act: Expanded credits for wind, solar, storage, hydrogen; supports AES’ 51 GW U.S. renewables pipeline; HLBV accounting impacts timing of tax credit recognition; $246 million Adjusted PTC realized in 2022; higher amounts expected in 2023; guidance pending creates uncertainty.
  - Global tax developments: Potentially material impacts from Chilean tax proposals, U.S. 15% corporate alternative minimum tax, and EU Pillar 2 15% global minimum tax beginning 2024.
  - Inflation: Higher rates may raise costs; many international contracts indexed, U.S. generation generally not; utility cost recovery subject to regulatory timing.
  - Reference rate reform: Transition from USD LIBOR to SOFR; fallback protocols and contract amendments underway.
  - Puerto Rico (PREPA Title III): PPAs continue with payments largely current; AES Puerto Rico and AES Ilumina non-recourse debt in technical default, classified current; mediation ongoing; $96 million long-lived assets considered recoverable.
- Decarbonization initiatives:
  - Strategy shifting to renewables, storage, LNG, modernized grids; intent to exit coal by year-end 2025 (subject to approvals).
  - Regulatory/offtaker pressures in Chile, Puerto Rico, Bulgaria, Hawaii; potential for material financial effects (useful lives, capital needs) not yet estimable.
- Regulatory updates:
  - AES Maritza PPA review by EU DG Comp for State Aid compliance; discussions with Bulgaria’s government ongoing; outcomes range from PPA continuation to termination with compensation; carrying value $427 million; material adverse outcome possible.
  - AES Ohio: PUCO approved $76 million base distribution revenue increase to take effect with new Electric Security Plan (ESP 4) filing seeking grid upgrades and recovery of regulatory assets; decision expected in 2023.
  - AES Indiana IRP (2022): Plan to convert remaining Petersburg coal units to natural gas by end of 2025 and add up to 1,300 MW of wind/solar/storage by 2027.
- Foreign exchange exposure noted across multiple countries.
- Impairments:
  - 2022 asset and other-than-temporary impairments of $938 million; post-impairment carrying value of assessed assets/equity affiliates $1.5 billion.
  - Goodwill impairment of $777 million at AES Andes and AES El Salvador due to higher discount rates/country risk and lower energy price forecasts; other reporting units not currently at risk but subject to future changes.
- Capital resources and liquidity (as of December 31, 2022):
  - Unrestricted cash $1.4 billion ($24 million at parent/qualified holdings); short-term investments $730 million; restricted cash/debt service reserves $713 million.
  - Debt: $19.4 billion non-recourse and $3.9 billion recourse outstanding; $1.8 billion current non-recourse debt (primarily due within 12 months) including $177 million in technical default (non-payment related), with $170 million attributable to matters not fully detailed in the excerpt.

structure.title: Capital Resources and Liquidity
structure.heading: Capital Resources and Liquidity
structure.start_phrase: As of December 31, 2022, the Company had unrestricted cash and cash equivalents of $1.4 billion, of which $24 million was held at the Parent Company and qualified holding companies.
structure.summary:
- Regulatory and resource planning updates: AES Ohio proposed ESP 4 to enhance service reliability, price stability, invest in local economic development, and recover certain regulatory assets, without continuing the Rate Stabilization Charge; PUCO approval expected in 2023. AES Indiana’s 2022 IRP plans to convert remaining Petersburg coal units to natural gas by end-2025 and add up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery storage by 2027.
- Market and FX exposure: Operations across multiple countries create exposure to foreign exchange volatility; additional market risk details referenced elsewhere in the report.
- Impairments: Recognized $938 million of long-lived asset and equity affiliate impairments in 2022; post-impairment carrying value for assessed assets was $1.5 billion. Recorded $777 million goodwill impairment due to higher discount rates, increased country risk premiums, and lower forecast energy prices and macro assumptions (notably in Colombia), eliminating goodwill at AES Andes and AES El Salvador. Other reporting units showed >10% fair value headroom but remain subject to future risk.
- Capital resources and liquidity: As of December 31, 2022, unrestricted cash was $1.4 billion (only $24 million at the Parent/qualified holding companies), with $730 million in short-term investments and $713 million in restricted cash. Debt totaled $19.4 billion non-recourse and $3.9 billion recourse; current non-recourse debt was $1.8 billion, largely due within 12 months, with $177 million in technical (non-payment) defaults, $170 million tied to an offtaker bankruptcy. Supplier financing obligations were $662 million. The company employs project-level non-recourse financing, targets a majority of fixed-rate debt (using swaps), and manages interest rate exposure (about $6 billion variable unhedged consolidated; Parent’s unhedged variable exposure includes $325 million under its revolver and a $200 million term loan). Brazil maintains $2 billion in floating-rate exposure as an inflation hedge.
- Credit support and letters of credit: Parent guarantees and other credit support totaled approximately $2.4 billion; letters of credit outstanding were $128 million (unsecured facilities), $123 million (bilateral), and $34 million (revolver), with fees of 1%–3% annually.
- Financing strategy and risks: Continued reliance on non-recourse project finance where available; inability to secure such funding or provide additional support could result in subsidiary insolvency or loss of investment. Subsidiaries’ access to capital markets and regulatory timing affect liquidity.
- Long-term receivables: About $303 million of noncurrent receivables (primarily Chile stabilization fund recoveries and a U.S. heat rate call option premium due in 2024). A $1 billion long-term loan receivable related to the Mong Duong (Vietnam) BOT project reverted from held-for-sale to a loan receivable, net of CECL reserve.
- Cash flows and capital deployment:
  - 2022 sources and uses: Major sources included non-recourse debt issuances, revolver borrowings, operating cash flow, short-term investment sales, supplier financing, and sales to noncontrolling interests; major uses included revolver repayments, capital expenditures, non-recourse debt repayments, short-term investment purchases, acquisition of noncontrolling interests, and emissions allowance purchases.
  - Operating cash flow: 2022 vs. 2021 increased by $813 million; adjusted net income declined $260 million (lower margins in South America and U.S. & Utilities, higher interest expense) offset by working capital improvements of $1.1 billion. 2021 vs. 2020 decreased by $853 million, driven by higher working capital needs despite higher adjusted net income.
  - Investing cash flow: 2022 vs. 2021 decreased by $2.8 billion (higher capex, increased emissions allowances in Bulgaria, and net short-term investment purchases at AES Brasil). Growth capex rose sharply for renewables and T&D across AES Clean Energy, AES Brasil, AES Indiana, and AES Ohio; maintenance capex modestly higher; environmental spend flat. 2021 vs. 2020 investing outflows also increased (more acquisitions, equity affiliate funding, and capex focused on renewables and T&D).
  - Financing cash flow: 2022 vs. 2021 increased by $3.0 billion, driven by higher non-recourse borrowings, greater use of non-recourse revolvers, increased sales to noncontrolling interests (including tax equity and partial Southland sale), and higher net supplier financing; offset by absence of 2021 Parent Equity Units issuance and higher acquisitions of noncontrolling interests (notably additional AES Andes stake). 2021 vs. 2020 improved mainly due to Equity Units issuance and higher Parent revolver usage.
- Parent Company liquidity and covenants: Year-end 2022 Parent Company Liquidity was $1.165 billion (cash at Parent/qualified holding companies plus revolver availability net of borrowings and LCs). Recourse debt was $3.9 billion; the Parent paid $0.63 per share in dividends during 2022. Liquidity outlook is adequate subject to capital market access, subsidiary performance, FX, power prices, and regulatory outcomes; Parent remained in covenant compliance.
- Non-recourse debt defaults and cross-default considerations: Certain subsidiaries (AES Puerto Rico, AES Ilumina, AES Jordan Solar) were in technical default (no payment defaults) totaling $177 million; none qualified as material subsidiaries for Parent cross-default provisions as of year-end, though future changes could alter this assessment.
- Contractual and contingent obligations: Total contractual obligations of $63.6 billion (including debt, interest, leases, electricity and fuel purchase commitments, and other purchase obligations) across varying maturities. Parent contingent obligations totaled $2.7 billion (guarantees, letters of credit, surety bonds), largely performance-related and only payable upon specific contingencies.
- Critical accounting policies: Emphasis on income taxes, including judgmental reserves for uncertain tax positions, exposure to audits, sensitivity of effective tax rate to geographic earnings mix, and potential adverse impacts from tax law or enforcement changes.

structure.title: Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates
structure.heading: Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates
structure.start_phrase: The Consolidated Financial Statements of AES are prepared in conformity with U.S. GAAP, which requires the use of estimates, judgments, and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the periods presented.
structure.summary:
- Summary of parent company contingent contractual obligations as of December 31, 2022, totaling $2.693 billion across 140 agreements, including guarantees and commitments, various letters of credit (unsecured, bilateral, revolving), and surety bonds, with noted maximum exposure ranges per agreement and a caveat excluding standard reps and warranties.
- Description of performance-related contingent obligations, key risk drivers (e.g., change of control, construction overruns, subsidiary default, political risk, tax indemnities, market power prices, sponsor support, liquidated damages), and acknowledgment that while material funding is not expected, outcomes are uncertain and could require substantial payments.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates under U.S. GAAP, highlighting areas requiring significant judgment:
  - Income taxes: uncertain tax positions, examinations, impact of geographic earnings mix, policy elections (GILTI expensed, AMT not considered in DTA realizability), and indefinitely reinvested earnings.
  - Impairments: identification of indicators, fair value measurement judgment, sensitivity to assumptions.
  - Depreciation: useful life determinations and periodic reassessment.
  - Fair value measurements: financial instruments (investments, derivatives) and nonfinancial assets/liabilities using DCF models, market-sourced assumptions, and discount rate selection.
  - Derivative accounting and hedging: inclusion of nonperformance and credit risk, valuation models, and curve extrapolations.
  - Regulatory assets: recoverability assessments.
  - Consolidation: VIE vs. voting model determinations and evaluation of substantive vs. protective rights.
  - Pension and other postretirement plans: funded status recognition and key assumptions.
  - Revenue recognition: performance obligations for energy and capacity, over-time recognition via output methods and right-to-invoice.
  - Leases: recognition of right-of-use assets and liabilities using incremental borrowing rates.
  - Credit losses: expected loss model for receivables and securities.
- Reference to new accounting pronouncements adopted and issued (details in Note 1).
- Quantitative and qualitative market risk disclosures:
  - Exposure to commodity prices (power, oil, gas, coal, environmental credits), foreign exchange due to multi-country operations, and interest rate fluctuations.
  - Commodity price risk management via physical and financial hedges (futures, swaps, options), noting residual exposures from short-term sales and imperfect indexation.
  - 2023 sensitivity to a 10% uncorrelated commodity move: approximately $5 million gain for power, $10 million loss for oil, and $5 million loss for coal and natural gas; downside scenario linked to lower power/oil and higher gas/coal prices; exposure expected to evolve as contracts and hedges change, generally increasing in later years with reduced hedge levels.

structure.title: QUANTIT ATIVE AND QUALIT ATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
structure.heading: ITEM 7A. QUANTIT ATIVE AND QUALIT ATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
structure.start_phrase: Our businesses are exposed to and proactively manage market risk.
structure.summary:
- Highlights application of a forward-looking expected credit loss model (CECL) for trade and other receivables, HTM debt securities, loans, and other instruments; for AFS debt securities, credit-related unrealized losses are recorded as an allowance with a corresponding earnings impact.
- References Note 1 for detailed Significant Accounting Policies and recently adopted/issued accounting pronouncements not yet effective.
- Introduces Item 7A market risk overview, noting exposure to commodity prices (electricity, oil, natural gas, coal, environmental credits), foreign exchange volatility across multiple currencies, and interest rate fluctuations; includes safe harbor under Securities Act Section 27A and Exchange Act Section 21E and cross-references Risk Factors.
- Describes commodity price risk management via physical and financial contracts, futures, swaps, and options; acknowledges residual unhedged exposures from imperfect indexation, short-term sales, and fuel pass-throughs.
- Provides 2023 commodity sensitivity: a 10% uncorrelated move implies approximately a $5 million gain for power, and losses of about $10 million for oil and $5 million for coal and natural gas; aggregate downside with lower power/oil and higher gas/coal prices; notes changing exposures over time as hedges/contracting evolve.
- Explains that commodity impacts vary by market factors (hydrology, supply/demand, regional fuel dynamics, competition, regulation) and operational flexibility; volume variability from weather/economy affects spot exposure.
- Segment specifics:
  - US and Utilities: largely contracted generation; Southland Legacy Assets permitted through end of 2023 with capacity contracts and added energy value.
  - South America: Chile PPAs mostly indexed to coal; hedging with international coal instruments for non-indexed portions; Colombia has spot exposure for uncontracted hydro volumes; Brazil hydro covered by contracts with a regulated sharing mechanism that may be insufficient in dry conditions, potentially requiring spot purchases.
  - MCAC: Panama highly contracted with hydrology-driven variance; Dominican Republic gas plants under portfolio contracts with potential spot market buys/sells due to mismatches.
  - Eurasia: Vietnam and Bulgaria have minimal commodity price exposure due to limited merchant exposure and fuel pass-through mechanisms.
- Details foreign exchange risk from operations in currencies including ARS, BRL, CLP, COP, DOP, EUR, and MXN; mitigation via revenue indexation and FX forwards, swaps, and options.
- States AES’ FX hedging prioritizes protecting cash flows and reducing earnings volatility, though timing/amount mismatches may leave residual earnings volatility; largest 2023 FX risks are BRL and EUR.
- Provides 10% USD appreciation sensitivity on 2023 cash distributions (net of hedges): less than $10 million gain (BRL), less than $5 million gain (COP), and less than $5 million loss (EUR); notes sensitivities exclude transactional gains/losses and may change; do not reflect market restrictions/inconvertibility.
- Outlines interest rate risk from variable/fixed debt and derivatives (swaps, caps, floors); financing mix aligned with revenue characteristics; most exposure in non-recourse project debt.
- Provides 2023 interest rate sensitivity: a one-time 100 bps increase would raise pre-tax interest expense by less than $55 million across ARS, BRL, CLP, COP, EUR, and USD debt.
- Item 8 notes auditor information: Ernst & Young LLP (Tysons, Virginia), PCAOB ID 42; indicates inclusion of Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.

structure.title: FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENT ARY DATA
structure.heading: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENT ARY DATA
structure.start_phrase: Our auditors are Ernst & Young LLP, located in Tysons, Virginia.
structure.summary:
- Excerpt from Item 8 of The AES Corporation’s 2022 Annual Report covering the independent auditor’s report and consolidated balance sheets.
- Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm: Ernst & Young LLP (PCAOB ID 42), Tysons, Virginia.
- Unqualified opinion on the consolidated financial statements for the three years ended December 31, 2022, stating they present fairly in conformity with U.S. GAAP.
- Unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022, based on COSO 2013.
- Basis for opinion outlines auditor independence, responsibilities, PCAOB standards, and audit procedures.

- Critical Audit Matters:
  - Goodwill impairment testing for AES Andes and AES El Salvador:
    - Quantitative test using an income approach; key assumptions include discount rates driven by interest rates and country risk premiums.
    - Fair values were below carrying amounts; AES recorded $777 million of goodwill impairment in Q4 2022.
    - Audit response included testing controls, methodologies, key assumptions, data completeness/accuracy, sensitivity analyses, and use of valuation specialists.
  - Long-lived asset impairments and useful-life re-evaluations:
    - Complex due to diverse geographies, regulatory/economic factors, and AES’s decarbonization transition.
    - Impairment expense of $661 million recognized for Maritza and TEG TEP asset groups in 2022.
    - Significant estimates included revenue growth and discount rates; auditors tested controls, assessed impairment indicators, evaluated useful lives (including PPAs), industry/regulatory trends, valuation methods, and performed sensitivity analyses with specialist support.

- Consolidated Balance Sheets (December 31, 2022 vs. 2021) highlights:
  - Total assets increased to $38.4 billion from $33.0 billion.
  - Current assets $7.6 billion; cash and cash equivalents $1.37 billion; short-term investments $0.73 billion.
  - Property, plant and equipment, net rose to $23.0 billion; construction in progress $4.62 billion.
  - Goodwill decreased to $0.36 billion from $1.18 billion, reflecting impairments; other intangibles $1.84 billion; new loan receivable $1.05 billion.
  - Total current liabilities $6.5 billion; total noncurrent liabilities $26.0 billion.
  - Debt composition: recourse debt $3.9 billion; non-recourse debt approximately $19.6 billion (current and noncurrent combined).
  - Redeemable stock of subsidiaries $1.32 billion.
  - Total equity $4.50 billion, including AES stockholders’ equity $2.44 billion and noncontrolling interests $2.07 billion; accumulated deficit widened, while accumulated other comprehensive loss improved.

structure.title: Consolidated Balance Sheets
structure.heading: Consolidated Balance Sheets
structure.summary:
- Content covered: Consolidated Balance Sheets as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and Consolidated Statements of Operations for the years ended 2022, 2021, and 2020 for The AES Corporation.

- Scale and growth:
  - Total assets increased to $38.4B from $33.0B year over year, driven by higher current assets and significant investment in property, plant and equipment (notably construction in progress).
  - Total liabilities rose to $32.5B from $27.1B, primarily from higher non-recourse debt.
  - Total equity was roughly flat/slightly lower at $4.5B (from $4.6B), with AES stockholders’ equity down to $2.44B and noncontrolling interests up to $2.07B.

- Balance sheet highlights:
  - Current assets rose to $7.64B (from $5.36B): higher cash and equivalents, restricted cash, short-term investments, receivables, inventory, and other current assets; current held-for-sale assets declined.
  - Property, plant and equipment, net increased to $23.0B (from $19.9B), with construction in progress up markedly ($4.62B vs $2.41B).
  - Goodwill decreased substantially ($362M vs $1.18B), indicating impairments/disposals; noncurrent held-for-sale assets were eliminated.
  - A new loan receivable of $1.05B appeared in other assets; CECL allowances noted in current and noncurrent other assets.
  - Liabilities: non-recourse debt expanded materially (total current and noncurrent $19.6B vs $15.0B), including amounts related to variable interest entities; recourse debt modestly higher at $3.9B.
  - Accumulated deficit widened and additional paid-in capital declined; accumulated other comprehensive loss improved (less negative); treasury stock slightly lower.

- Operations and performance:
  - Revenue grew to $12.6B in 2022 (from $11.1B in 2021 and $9.7B in 2020), with non-regulated businesses contributing the majority; regulated revenue also increased.
  - Total cost of sales rose, and operating margin slipped to $2.55B (from $2.71B).
  - Significant charges in 2022: goodwill impairment ($777M), asset impairment ($763M), higher interest expense, and other non-operating expense; modest loss on disposal.
  - 2021 included large asset impairments ($1.58B) and a major loss on disposal/sale of business interests ($1.68B).
  - Results: net loss from continuing operations of $505M in 2022 (vs $955M loss in 2021; $149M income in 2020). Net loss attributable to AES was $546M in 2022 (vs $409M loss in 2021; $46M income in 2020).
  - EPS (basic/diluted) for AES common stockholders: $(0.82) in 2022, $(0.61) in 2021, $0.07 in 2020.
  - Income tax moved from a benefit in 2021 to an expense in 2022; equity in losses of affiliates increased; noncontrolling interests and redeemable stock allocations affected the net loss attributable to AES.

- Other:
  - Commitments and contingencies referenced.
  - Held-for-sale assets and liabilities decreased year over year.

structure.title: General and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
structure.heading: Note 1 - General and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
structure.start_phrase: The AES Corporation is a holding company (the "Parent Company") that, through its subsidiaries and affiliates, (collectively, "AES" or "the Company") operates a geographically diversified portfolio of electricity generation and distribution businesses.
structure.summary:
- Overview and basis of presentation: AES Corporation is a holding company operating a diversified global portfolio of generation and distribution businesses. Financial statements are prepared under U.S. GAAP; most operating entity liabilities are non-recourse to the parent.
- Consolidation and investments: Consolidates controlled subsidiaries and VIEs where AES is primary beneficiary; equity method used when AES has significant influence without control. Intercompany eliminated. Basis differences at equity investees are amortized through equity income; other-than-temporary impairments recorded in other non-operating expense.
- Noncontrolling interests and redeemable equity: NCI presented in equity with income and OCI attributed separately; losses continue to be attributed to NCI even below zero. Equity securities with redemption features outside issuer control are temporary equity; measurement depends on redemption probability; mandatorily redeemable instruments are liabilities.
- Business combinations and disposals: Accounting for acquisitions/disposals of businesses, assets, or equity interests; impairment limited to long-lived assets on execution of sales agreements; gains/losses on completion recorded in results, including CTA reclassification.
- Profit-sharing/HLBV: For certain U.S. renewables partnerships, earnings allocated using the hypothetical liquidation at book value method, including recognition of “Day one gain” impacts tied to ITCs.
- Estimates: Significant estimates include asset lives, impairments, AROs, credit losses, fair values in business combinations and VIE acquisitions, HLBV allocations, pensions, lease IBRs, environmental liabilities, regulatory items, and litigation.
- Held-for-sale and discontinued operations: Measurement at lower of carrying amount or fair value less cost to sell; classification and presentation guidance; discontinued operations reported separately, with prior periods recast and gains/losses on disposal included.
- Fair value measurement: Exit price framework with Level 1–3 hierarchy; applied to marketable securities, derivatives, and certain nonfinancial measurements (e.g., business combinations, impairments, AROs). Transfers between levels at period-end.
- Liquidity and cash: Cash equivalents are original maturities of three months or less; restricted cash defined by contractual limits. At Dec 31, 2022: cash and cash equivalents $1,374m; restricted cash $536m; debt service reserves/other deposits $177m; total $2,087m (vs. $1,484m in 2021).
- Marketable securities: Composition includes debentures, CDs, government debt, and money market funds. HTM debt at amortized cost with CECL; AFS debt FV with non-credit changes in OCI and credit losses through allowance; equity securities FV through earnings.
- Receivables and CECL: Accounts/notes receivable at amortized cost with expected credit losses under ASC 326 recognized primarily in cost of sales; interest recognized on accrual unless not assured; write-offs when uncollectible.
- Inventory: Fuel/raw materials and spare parts at lower of cost or NRV, primarily average cost; impair fuel if not recoverable; spares reduced for obsolescence. At Dec 31, 2022: total $1,055m (fuel/raw $733m; spares $322m).
- Long-lived assets: PPE at cost less depreciation; capitalization of construction-related costs when completion probable; maintenance expensed; subsidies/LDs/ITCs reduce PPE. Depreciation straight-line considering salvage and AROs; treatment of capital/rotable spares; concession assets depreciated using contract-specific estimates (not ASC 853). Finite-lived intangibles amortized (1–50 years); purchased emission allowances treated as intangibles; impairments tested via undiscounted cash flows then FV.
- Debt issuance costs: Presented net against debt (except revolvers as assets); amortized via effective interest method; make-whole payments in financing cash flows.
- Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles: Annual (Oct 1) or triggering-event impairment tests; qualitative or quantitative approaches; goodwill impairment limited to carrying amount of goodwill; indefinite-lived intangibles (e.g., land/water rights) impaired if carrying amount exceeds FV.
- Payables and accrued liabilities: Trade payables for core operations; other accrued includes taxes, regulatory liabilities, legal contingencies, payroll/benefits. Includes $662m supplier financing arrangements (with $296m parent guarantee); related interest in interest expense or capitalized.
- Regulatory accounting: Recognition and recoverability assessment of regulatory assets and liabilities; returns on regulatory assets recorded as interest income.
- Pensions/OPEB: Recognize funded status on balance sheet with actuarial changes in OCI (or through rates at certain regulated utilities); YE measurement date; assets at FV.
- Income taxes: Deferreds for temporary differences with valuation allowances as needed; uncertain tax positions recognized using more-likely-than-not threshold; interest/penalties in tax expense. Elections: GILTI as period expense; ITCs flow-through; AOCL reclassification on a portfolio basis; do not consider CAMT effects in realizability assessment until incurred.
- Asset retirement obligations: Recognize at FV when incurred; accretion and depreciation recorded; gain/loss on settlement.
- Foreign currency: Functional currency translation to USD with balance sheet rates and average income statement rates; CTA in OCI, reclassified on sale or substantial liquidation; long-term intercompany FX also in OCI.
- Revenue recognition (ASC 606):
  - Utilities: Regulated tariffs; typically a single series performance obligation satisfied over time; output method by MWh delivered; ISO/RTO net presentation when settled net hourly; billing agent presentation net when applicable.
  - Generation: Contracts may include distinct energy, capacity, and services; allocation based on standalone selling price; capacity recognized over time (often right-to-invoice expedient); energy recognized on output; performance bonuses/penalties as variable consideration; lease components identified and allocated under ASC 842; ISO spot transactions presented net by hour. Construction services revenue recognized over time; significant financing components recorded as long-term receivables with interest income.
  - Contract balances: Accounts receivable include billed and unbilled; contract liabilities in accrued and other or other noncurrent liabilities. Remaining performance obligation disclosures apply ASC 606 practical expedients (exclude <1 year, right-to-invoice, and certain variable consideration).
- Leases (ASC 842):
  - Lessee: Recognize ROU assets and lease liabilities at PV of payments using incremental borrowing rate; short-term leases expensed straight-line; options included when reasonably certain.
  - Lessor: Certain capacity elements treated as operating leases with straight-line lease revenue; BESS arrangements often sales-type leases with derecognition of asset and recognition of net investment.
- Share-based compensation: RSUs, PSUs, PCUs, options; grant-date FV expensed straight-line net of forfeitures; options valued via Black-Scholes.
- G&A expenses: Corporate functions and business development not allocable to segments.
- Derivatives and hedging (ASC 815): Recognize derivatives at FV unless NPNS; common hedges include interest rate swaps (cash flow hedges), FX contracts, and commodity hedges (often economic). Hedge gains/losses deferred in OCI and reclassified when hedged items affect earnings; ineffectiveness ends hedge accounting prospectively. Earnings classification by risk type; operating cash flow classification except certain construction-period interest hedges in investing; no balance sheet offsetting.
- Credit losses (ASC 326) details and reserves:
  - CECL applies to receivables, certain lease investments, HTM debt, financial guarantees, and off-balance sheet credit exposures. Allowance reflects expected lifetime losses using historical, current, and forecast data.
  - 2022 CECL rollforward highlights: total allowance ended at $83m (notably Argentina receivables and a lease receivable at Southland Energy); excludes operating lease and dispute allowances.
- Recently adopted standards:
  - ASU 2021-05 (lessor variable payments): adopted prospectively; no material impact.
  - ASU 2020-06 (convertibles and equity contracts): adopted fully retrospectively; reclass within equity (increase preferred stock $13m; decrease APIC); no EPS impact.
  - Topic 848 (reference rate reform): adopted prospectively; no material impact.
- ASC 326 adoption impacts (Jan 1, 2020):
  - Mong Duong II (Vietnam) BOT loan receivable: established CECL reserve of $34m based on sovereign default/recovery benchmarks and asset-specific factors.
  - Argentina exposures (CAMMESA and related financing receivables): established CECL reserve of $29m using sovereign default/recovery data and asset-specific adjustments.
  - Other assets: no material CECL impact due to short-term nature/turnover and lease scope exclusions.
- New standards issued, not yet effective:
  - ASU 2021-08 (Topic 805) on contract assets/liabilities in business combinations: evaluating impact.
  - ASU 2022-04 (supplier finance programs) enhanced disclosures: to be adopted in 2023; rollforward disclosure effective 2024.
- Additional quantitative disclosures included:
  - Supplier finance obligation balance and guarantee.
  - Cash/restricted cash reconciliation.
  - Inventory composition and balance.
  - CECL allowance rollforwards by asset category.
- Next section previewed: Property, plant and equipment components and useful lives (details follow beyond this excerpt).

structure.title: Fair V alue

structure.start_phrase: The fair value of current financial assets and liabilities, debt service reserves, and other deposits approximate their reported carrying amounts.
structure.summary:
- Asset retirement obligations increased due to acquisitions and operational changes:
  - 2022: Higher obligations at AES Brasil from initial recognition tied to the Cubico II acquisition.
  - 2021: Increases at AES Clean Energy (New York Wind acquisition) and in Chile (shortened useful lives at Ventanas and Angamos coal plants, Andes Solar 2b development, and upward cash flow revisions at Los Cururos).

- Fair value policy overview (Note 5):
  - Valuation approaches: market, income (DCF-based), and cost; investments generally valued via market approach; derivatives via income approach; nonfinancial assets often valued via income approach in impairments.
  - Derivatives fair value methodology includes observable inputs when available; extrapolation of forward curves and proxy inputs used when not; credit valuation adjustments (CVA) reflect counterparty and company nonperformance risk.
  - Fair value hierarchy application: Level 3 classification when unobservable inputs significantly affect values; transfers between Levels 2 and 3 occur with changes in input significance.
  - Fair value considerations include data sources (e.g., Bloomberg/Reuters), market liquidity assessment, and nonperformance risk.

- Recurring fair value measurements:
  - Investments (as of 12/31/22): Available-for-sale debt securities $701 million (primarily certificates of deposit, all maturing within one year); equity securities (mutual funds) $38 million. No impairments recognized in 2022 or 2021; AFS sales proceeds were $1,065 million (2022), $578 million (2021), $582 million (2020).
  - Derivatives (as of 12/31/22): Assets $645 million; liabilities $474 million. Notable shift vs. 2021 includes interest rate derivatives moving to a net asset position ($314 million assets vs. $6 million liabilities in 2022, compared with $53 million assets and $294 million liabilities in 2021).
  - Total assets at fair value: $1,384 million (2022) vs. $476 million (2021). Total liabilities: $474 million (2022) vs. $384 million (2021).

- Level 3 derivative activity and key unobservable inputs:
  - 2022 Level 3 net balance ended at $17 million (driven by foreign currency derivatives, partially offset by commodity positions).
  - Significant unobservable inputs:
    - Argentine peso derivatives: long-dated ARS/USD exchange rates.
    - CAISO energy swap: forward power prices beyond 2030.
  - Earnings impacts disclosed for unrealized gains/losses on Level 3 instruments held at period-end.

- Nonrecurring fair value measurements (impairments and disposals):
  - 2022 impairments/fair value remeasurements:
    - Long-lived assets held and used: Maritza and TEG TEP measured using DCF with significant assumptions (annual revenue growth, variable margin, discount rates).
    - Held-for-sale: Jordan disposal group measured at fair value less cost to sell.
    - Goodwill: AES Andes and AES El Salvador measured, resulting in goodwill impairments.
    - Equity method investment: sPower measured via DCF (dividend growth and discount rate assumptions).
  - 2021 impairments/fair value remeasurements:
    - Long-lived assets: Puerto Rico, Mountain View I & II, Ventanas 3 & 4, Angamos, and Buffalo Gap I–III.
    - Disposals/held-for-sale: Estrella del Mar I; Alto Maipo (fair value used for goodwill allocation in loss on disposal).
  - Detailed tables present levels within the hierarchy and pre-tax losses.

- Financial instruments not measured at fair value (fair value disclosures):
  - 12/31/22: Noncurrent accounts receivable carrying $301 million (fair value $340 million, Level 3); non-recourse debt carrying $19,429 million (fair value $18,527 million; predominantly Level 2 with a Level 3 component); recourse debt carrying $3,894 million (fair value $3,505 million, Level 2).
  - Disclosures note receivables tied to Chile’s Stabilization Fund and Argentina’s CAMMESA.

- Derivative instruments and hedging activities (Note 6):
  - Notional exposures and maturities:
    - Interest rate derivatives up to $6,040 million, latest maturity 2059.
    - Cross-currency swaps (BRL) $293 million, to 2034.
    - FX derivatives across EUR, CLP, COP, BRL, ARS with maturities through 2026.
    - Commodity derivatives: natural gas (MMBtu) to 2030, power (MWh) to 2040, coal to 2027.
  - Fair value by designation (12/31/22):

- Derivatives and AOCL activity (2022, 2021, 2020):

- Financing receivables:
  - Summary table by country as of December 31, 2022 vs. 2021: Net receivables increased to $303m from $57m, led by Chile ($239m vs. $17m), U.S. ($46m from $0), Argentina ($5m vs. $10m), and Other ($13m vs. $30m); allowance largely nil in 2022.

These receivables are ARS-denominated but USD-indexed, creating a foreign currency derivative; related derivative assets were $64m (2022) and $108m (2021). Historic collections since plants began operations (2010, 2016) considered in collectability assessments.

- Investments in and advances to affiliates (equity method):

  - sPower transactions: In Feb 2021, AES merged sPower and AES Renewable Holdings development platforms into AES Clean Energy Development (consolidated), decreasing sPower’s carrying value by $102m and recognizing a $214m gain in other income. In Dec 2021, AES acquired an additional 25% interest in specified sPower development projects, recognizing a $35m gain, resulting in 75% ownership in those projects via the consolidated platform while retaining 50% ownership in the sPower equity method investment.

structure.title: Investments in and Advances to Affiliates
structure.heading: Note 8 - Investments in and Advances to Affiliates
structure.start_phrase:
The following table summarizes the relevant effective equity ownership interest and carrying values for the Company's investments
accounted for under the equity method as of the periods indicated:
structure.summary:
- Notes discuss receivables and related risks in Argentina, including FONINVEMEM agreements under which AES Argentina contributed receivables to finance generation projects. These peso-denominated receivables are indexed to USD, creating a foreign currency derivative that offsets devaluation-related losses over time. Fair value of the related derivative assets was $64 million at December 31, 2022 ($108 million in 2021). Collections have been ongoing since plants began operations in 2010 and 2016. The company monitors macroeconomic, regulatory, and credit risks and accrues interest once recognition criteria are met.
- A call option premium related to Southland Energy CCGT units is expected to be received in 2024.
- Investments in and advances to affiliates (equity method) totaled $952 million at December 31, 2022 (down from $1,080 million in 2021). Key holdings and ownership: sPower (50%), Fluence (about 34% to 33.5% by year-end 2022), Grupo Energía Gas Panamá (49%), Uplight (about 29%), Energía Natural Dominicana Enadom (effective 43% through an 85%-owned subsidiary), Mesa La Paz (50%), Barry (100% but a VIE not consolidated), and other affiliates.
- sPower: AES merged the sPower and AES Renewable Holdings development platforms in 2021 into AES Clean Energy Development (consolidated), recognizing gains of $214 million (platform carve-out) and $35 million (additional 25% in select projects). In December 2022, AES agreed to sell 49% of an indirect interest in a portfolio of sPower operating assets (closed February 28, 2023) and recorded a $175 million other-than-temporary impairment, establishing a $432 million fair value for its sPower investment. sPower remains an equity method investment, reported in US and Utilities.
- Alto Maipo: Emerged from Chapter 11 in May 2022; treated as a VIE. AES is not the primary beneficiary and elected the fair value option; the investment’s fair value at December 31, 2022 was insignificant. Reported in South America.
- Fluence: QIA invested $125 million in June 2021, reducing AES’s stake from 50% to 43.2% and generating a $60 million gain. Fluence’s November 1, 2021 IPO further reduced AES’s stake to 34.2% with a $325 million gain; equity dilution and share-based awards reduced AES’s stake to 33.5% by December 31, 2022. Fluence remains equity method, reported in Corporate and Other.
- Uplight: 2021 transactions included AES contributions of $37 million (ownership down to 29.6%) and $23 million (ownership to 29.4%), with a $25 million loss recognized, mainly from share-based awards and transaction costs. Continues under equity method, reported in Corporate and Other.
- Gas Natural Atlántico II: AES acquired the remaining interest in September 2021, remeasured to fair value, and recognized a $6 million gain; now consolidated and reported in MCAC.
- Grupo Energía Gas Panamá: 49% JV acquired the Gatun CCGT project in April 2021; AES contributed $45 million through 2022; accounted for under the equity method in MCAC.
- Guacolda: 2020 investee-level impairment reduced AES’s basis to zero and drove $127 million of equity losses; AES sold its 50% stake in July 2021 for $34 million, recognizing a $34 million gain. Previously in South America.

structure.title: Equity

structure.summary:
- Temporary equity and consolidation matters:
  - Potengi (South America SBU): In March 2022, BRF bought 24% for $12 million, reducing AES’ indirect ownership to 35.5%. AES retained control; BRF holds a put option at PPA end, so NCI is classified as temporary equity under ASC 810, with redemption value changes recognized against permanent equity per ASC 480-10-S99.
  - Colon (MCAC SBU): In September 2021, AES acquired the remaining 49.9%, eliminating temporary equity; transaction decreased Parent Company Stockholders’ Equity by $12 million.
  - AES Clean Energy Development (US and Utilities SBU): Effective February 1, 2021, merger of sPower and AES Renewable Holdings development platforms; AIMCo received 25% minority interest with exit rights, classified as temporary equity. Q2 2021 measurement adjustments increased temporary equity by $81 million. Future redemption value changes recognized against permanent equity per ASC 480-10-S99.

- Equity Units and mandatorily convertible preferred stock:
  - In March 2021, AES issued 10,430,500 Equity Units ($1.043 billion notional), each comprising a forward stock purchase contract (2024 Purchase Contracts) and a 10% interest in a share of 0% Series A Cumulative Perpetual Convertible Preferred Stock (Series A Preferred).
  - Accounting reassessment: Units treated as one combined unit of account (mandatorily convertible preferred stock); included in diluted EPS using the if-converted method. Q4 2021 corrections reclassified related balance sheet and equity statement amounts without impacting earnings, assets, cash flows, or segment info.
  - Proceeds: ~$1 billion net; $838 million attributed to Series A Preferred and $205 million to the present value of Contract Adjustment Payments (CAPs).
  - Key terms: Series A initially non-dividend-bearing, no accretion, perpetual with limited voting rights; pledged as collateral for 2024 Purchase Contracts; potential remarketing may increase dividend/conversion rate and modify earliest redemption date; redeemable at par plus unpaid dividends on/after March 22, 2024.
  - 2024 Purchase Contracts: Holders must purchase up to 57,292,650 common shares on February 15, 2024 for $100 each; anti-dilution applies. Initial max settlement rate 3.864; as of December 31, 2022, 3.8691 (reference price ~$25.85). Early cash settlement allowed at 85% of otherwise deliverable shares. Successful remarketing expected to yield ~$1 billion and issuance of Remarketed Series A Preferred.
  - CAPs: Paid at 6.875% per annum quarterly since May 15, 2021. The $205 million PV reduced Series A Preferred at inception; payments reduce the liability with ~$5 million total accretion to interest expense over three years. PV of CAPs was $89 million at December 31, 2022.

- Equity transactions with noncontrolling interests (NCI):
  - AES Clean Energy tax equity: 2022 sales of project interests to tax equity partners increased NCI by $230 million (prior years: $88 million in 2022 at AES Renewable Holdings? $127 million in 2021; $144 million in 2020).
  - Southland Energy (US and Utilities SBU): Sold 35% in 2020 for $424 million (retained 65%; earnings/losses to AES until March 1, 2021), increasing Parent Company Equity by $275 million. Sold additional 14.9% in December 2022 for $157 million, reducing economic interest to 50.1% and increasing Parent Company Equity by $91 million; AES continues consolidation.
  - AES Brasil (South America SBU): Incremental acquisitions in 2020–2021 raised AES’ indirect beneficial interest to 46.7%. 2022 private placement subscriptions increased interest to 47.4% with $98 million NCI contributions, APIC increase, and AOCL reclassifications. Reorganization to list on Novo Mercado completed March 2021; AES maintains board majority.
  - Chile Renovables (South America SBU): 49% sold to GIP in July 2021 for $53 million; continuing asset contributions in 2022 (Andes Solar 2a and Los Olmos) raised NCI by $96 million and APIC by $21 million; AES retains control.
  - Guaimbê Holding (South America SBU): 19.9% preferred shares issued in April 2021 for $158 million; additional 3.5% in January 2022 for $63 million; AES’ indirect ownership reduced to 35.8%; still consolidated.
  - AES Andes (South America SBU): 2020–2021 rights offering modestly increased AES’ interest (~67%); 2022 tender offer and follow-on purchases increased indirect beneficial interest to 99%, reducing Parent Company Equity by $172 million due to APIC decrease and AOCL reclassification.
  - Cochrane (South America SBU): September 2020 sale of preferred shares and 5% stake for $113 million; AES economic interest reduced to 38%; preferred holders have priority returns until recovery plus specified return; still consolidated.

- Net income and NCI transfers:
  - Net income (loss) attributable to AES: 2022 $(546) million; 2021 $(409) million; 2020 $46 million.
  - Transfers to/from NCI from share sales/purchases detailed, with net effect: 2022 $0; 2021 $(16) million; 2020 $171 million.

- Deconsolidations:
  - Alto Maipo: Chapter 11 filing in November 2021; AES deconsolidated the business, increasing Parent Company Equity by $182 million through removal of AOCL and accumulated deficit.

- Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss (AOCL):
  - AOCL by component moved from $(2,220) million at December 31, 2021 to $(1,640) million at December 31, 2022, driven largely by derivative gains.
  - Detailed reclassifications from AOCL to earnings presented, including impacts across revenue, cost of sales, interest expense, gains on disposals, impairments, FX, taxes, and attribution between AES and NCI.

- Dividends and share repurchases:
  - Common dividends: $0.1580 per share each quarter in 2022; on December 2, 2022, a $0.1659 quarterly dividend was declared, payable February 15, 2023.
  - Stock Repurchase Program: No repurchases in 2022; cumulative since 2010—154.3 million shares for $1.9 billion (avg. $12.12). $264 million remained authorized at December 31, 2022. Treasury stock totaled 150.0 million shares at year-end 2022; RSUs issued from treasury; no retirements.

- Segments and geographic information:
  - AES reports four operating/reportable segments aligned with SBUs: US and Utilities, South America, MCAC, and Eurasia. Corporate and Other includes self-insurance, certain equity affiliates, corporate overhead, and intercompany charges.

structure.summary:

- Reports balance sheet and investment metrics by segment:

  - Investments in and advances to affiliates: $952 million (2022); net equity in losses of affiliates $(71) million (2022), with Corporate and Other the primary driver of losses.
- Provides geographic information:

structure.title: Share-Based Compensation
structure.heading: Note 19 - Share-Based Compensation
structure.start_phrase: Restricted Stock Units — The Company issues RSUs under its long-term compensation plan.
structure.summary:
- Continuation of the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020, presenting segment and geographic disclosures.
- Segment information (US and Utilities, South America, MCAC, Eurasia, Corporate and Other) includes:
  - Total assets, depreciation and amortization, and capital expenditures by year.
  - Interest income and interest expense by year.
  - Investments in and advances to affiliates, and net equity in earnings (losses) of affiliates by year.
  - 2022 highlights: total assets $38.4B; capital expenditures $4.6B (up sharply from 2021); interest expense $1.1B vs. interest income $0.4B; net equity loss from affiliates $(71)M, with Corporate and Other a major driver of affiliate losses.
- Geographic information by country:
  - Total revenue for 2022, 2021, and 2020 and long-lived assets as of December 31, 2022 and 2021.
  - United States is the largest contributor; non-U.S. revenue totals $8.5B in 2022.
  - Significant non-U.S. markets include Chile, Dominican Republic, Panama, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, Vietnam, and Jordan; notable movement includes a decline in Bulgaria long-lived assets from 2021 to 2022.
  - Revenue is recognized in the country earned; assets are recorded where located.
  - Long-lived assets exclude intangibles and include property, plant and equipment and right-of-use assets for operating leases.
  - Puerto Rico revenues and assets are separately noted within totals.
  - Mong Duong II (Vietnam) is operated under a BOT contract; construction-related cash flows are recognized as a loan receivable (see Note 20—Revenue).
- Share-based compensation (Note 19) – Restricted Stock:
  - The company grants RSUs under its long-term incentive plan, typically based on a percentage of base salary.
  - RSUs generally vest over three years in equal annual installments.
  - RSUs are equity-settled; they do not entitle holders to, nor obligate the company for, cash settlement.

structure.title: Revenue
structure.heading: Note 20 - Revenue
structure.summary:
- Segment information for 2022, 2021, and 2020:
  - By Strategic Business Unit (US and Utilities, South America, MCAC, Eurasia, Corporate/Other): total assets, depreciation and amortization, and capital expenditures, plus interest income and expense.
  - Investments in and advances to affiliates and equity in earnings (losses) of affiliates by SBU, with Corporate/Other showing notable equity-method losses in 2022.

- Geographic disclosures:
  - Revenue by country and long-lived assets as of 2022 and 2021, with the United States as the largest market.
  - Significant non-U.S. operations include Chile, Dominican Republic, Panama, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia, Bulgaria, El Salvador, and others.

- Share-based compensation:
  - Restricted Stock Units (RSUs): typical three-year, ratable vesting; 2021–2022 awards to certain executives include an ESG performance modifier of ±15%.
  - Grant-date weighted average fair values per RSU for 2020–2022; RSU expense and tax effects; vesting/forfeiture activity; unrecognized compensation cost and expected amortization period; estimated forfeiture rate.
  - Other programs and expenses: stock options to non-employee directors (3-year vesting, 10-year term); Performance Stock Units (PFCF-based, 0–200% payout); Performance Cash Units (relative TSR vs indices, cash-settled with liability accounting).

- Revenue recognition (Note 20):
  - Disaggregation of revenue by SBU and by regulated vs non-regulated, separating revenue from contracts with customers and other non-ASC 606 revenue (leases/derivatives) for 2020–2022.
  - Contract balances: contract liabilities increased to $337 million at 12/31/22; revenue recognized from beginning liabilities disclosed.
  - Angamos (Chile) PPA early termination in 2020 created a $655 million contract liability, derecognized monthly through August 2021.
  - Mong Duong BOT financing: construction consideration accounted for as a loan receivable; classified held-for-sale at 12/31/21 and reclassified back to loan receivable at 12/31/22, with CECL reserves noted.
  - Remaining performance obligations: $9 million, primarily U.S. REC sales, with expected recognition over several years.

- Other income and expense (Note 21 introduction):
  - Describes typical components of other income (e.g., insurance recoveries, gains on sales, AFUDC) and other expense (partially shown, section continues).

structure.title: Other Income and Expense
structure.heading: Note 21 - Other Income and Expense
structure.start_phrase:
Other income generally includes gains on insurance recoveries in excess of property damage, gains on asset sales and liability
extinguishments, favorable judgments on contingencies, allowance for funds used during construction, and other income from miscellaneous
transactions.
structure.summary:
- 2020 revenue by segment and type: Provides regulated and non-regulated revenue by Strategic Business Unit (SBU). US and Utilities generated all regulated revenue ($2,661 million) and had total revenue of $3,918 million. Non-regulated revenue was: US and Utilities $1,257 million; South America $3,159 million; MCAC $1,766 million; Eurasia $828 million; Corporate and Eliminations $(11) million. Total 2020 revenue was $9,660 million. Other non-regulated revenue includes lease and derivative revenue not under ASC 606.
- Contract balances and liabilities: Contract liabilities were $337 million at December 31, 2022 and $216 million at December 31, 2021. Revenue recognized from beginning contract liabilities was $36 million in 2022 and $410 million in 2021.
- Angamos PPA termination (Chile): In August 2020, AES Andes agreed to early terminate two PPAs for the Angamos coal plant, recording a $655 million contract liability that was derecognized at $55 million per month through August 2021.
- Mong Duong financing arrangement (Vietnam): Under a BOT contract with a 25-year PPA, construction consideration is collected over the PPA term. As of December 31, 2021, the related loan receivable of $1.2 billion (net of $30 million CECL) was classified as held-for-sale. As of December 31, 2022, held-for-sale criteria were no longer met; the balance was reclassified to Loan receivable at $1.1 billion (net of $28 million CECL).
- Remaining performance obligations: $9 million of transaction price remained as of December 31, 2022, primarily fixed consideration for U.S. renewable energy credits, with about one-fifth expected to be recognized in 2023 and 2024 and the remainder thereafter.
- Other income and expense:
  - Definitions: Other income includes gains (e.g., insurance recoveries above property damage, asset sale gains, AFUDC, favorable legal outcomes). Other expense includes losses on asset sales/dispositions, legal contingencies, and other items.
  - Other income totaled $102 million (2022), $410 million (2021), and $75 million (2020). Key items include remeasurement gains (e.g., 5B in 2022; sPower development platform in 2021), insurance proceeds (TermoAndes in 2022), AFUDC, legal settlements (e.g., Alto Maipo in 2021), non-service pension income, gains on acquired customer contracts, contingent consideration remeasurement, and gains on asset sales (notably Redondo Beach land in 2020).
  - Other expense totaled $68 million (2022), $60 million (2021), and $53 million (2020). Key items include cost of disposition at AES Gilbert after a 2022 fire (including an allowance on a sales-type lease receivable), losses on asset sales/disposals, legal contingencies, losses at commencement of sales-type leases (AES Renewable Holdings), and loss on sale of Stabilization Fund receivables (AES Andes).
- Asset impairment expense:
  - Total impairments were $763 million (2022), $1,575 million (2021), and $864 million (2020).
  - Significant items by year:
    - 2022: Maritza ($468 million), TEG TEP ($193 million), Jordan ($76 million), Other ($26 million).
    - 2021: Ventanas 3 & 4 ($649 million), Puerto Rico ($475 million), Angamos ($155 million), Buffalo Gap III ($91 million), Buffalo Gap II ($73 million), Mountain View I & II ($67 million), Buffalo Gap I ($29 million), Estrella del Mar I ($11 million), Other ($25 million).
    - 2020: Angamos ($564 million), Ventanas 1 & 2 ($213 million), Hawaii ($38 million), Estrella del Mar I ($30 million), Other ($19 million).
  - TEG TEP: The October 1, 2022 annual goodwill impairment test failed, triggering a long-lived asset impairment. The asset group’s fair value was estimated at $311 million using an income approach.

structure.title: Asset Impairment Expense
structure.heading: Note 22 - Asset Impairment Expense

structure.summary:
- Breakdown of Other Income and Other Expense for 2022, 2021, and 2020, including totals and key components such as gains from remeasurement of investments and contingent consideration, insurance proceeds, AFUDC, legal settlements, gains on sales of assets, and various losses (dispositions, lease commencements, receivables sales). Footnotes explain notable items tied to specific projects and transactions (e.g., 5B, TermoAndes, Alto Maipo, sPower/AES Clean Energy, Great Cove Solar, Redondo Beach land, AES Gilbert fire, AES Renewable Holdings leases, AES Andes receivables).

- Asset Impairment Expense details by asset and year with totals (2022, 2021, 2020), including significant impairments at Maritza (Bulgaria coal phaseout), TEG TEP (goodwill-triggered long-lived asset impairment), Jordan (held-for-sale sale delay), Ventanas and Angamos (Chile decarbonization and early retirements), Buffalo Gap I/II/III (expired PPA and ERCOT market conditions), Mountain View I & II (repowering), Puerto Rico (coal legislative and operational risks), Estrella del Mar I (barge disconnection), and Hawaii (coal ban). Descriptions include fair value approaches, amounts, and reporting segments.

- Income Taxes: summary of current and deferred tax expense by federal, state, and foreign jurisdictions for 2022–2020; reconciliation of the U.S. statutory to effective tax rates highlighting major drivers such as taxes on foreign earnings, valuation allowance changes, uncertain tax positions, changes in tax law, investment tax credits, impacts from deconsolidations and impairments (including nondeductible goodwill impairments), and a noted item recorded to additional paid-in capital related to the Southland Energy ownership sale.

structure.title: Income Taxes
structure.heading: Note 23 - Income Taxes
structure.start_phrase: The following table summarizes the expense for income taxes on continuing operations for the periods indicated (in millions):
structure.summary:
- Asset impairments
  - Puerto Rico asset group fair value determined at $73 million, resulting in a pre-tax impairment expense of $475 million (US and Utilities SBU).

- Income taxes (Note 23)
  - Income tax provision: expense of $265 million (2022), benefit of $133 million (2021), expense of $216 million (2020).
  - Effective tax rate drivers:
    - 2022 ETR of (157)% driven primarily by nondeductible goodwill impairments at AES Andes and AES El Salvador (-127%), taxes on foreign earnings (-42%) influenced by favorable LNG sales and Argentina inflation/FX impacts. $27 million of tax expense recorded to APIC for a 2022 Southland interest sale excluded from ETR.
    - 2021 includes valuation allowance release (~$93 million) at a Brazilian subsidiary, benefit from closure of U.S. 2017 exam tied to TCJA transition tax (~$176 million), and impact of Alto Maipo deconsolidation (-17%) with related valuation allowance effects; Buffalo Gap impairment amounts allocated to tax equity noncontrolling interest were nondeductible (-3%).
    - 2020 includes tax benefit related to Guacolda equity investment and U.S. investment tax credit ($35 million for Na Pua Makani). $75 million tax expense to APIC for a 2020 Southland sale excluded from ETR.
  - Tax receivables/payables at year-end 2022: receivables $176 million; payables $104 million.
  - Deferred taxes:
    - U.S. federal NOLs ~$1.4 billion (mostly indefinite-lived); federal credits ~$70 million; state NOLs ~$6.1 billion; foreign NOLs ~$2.1 billion.
    - Valuation allowance $577 million at 12/31/22 (up $49 million, primarily from a Brazilian acquisition); decreased by $106 million in 2021 due to a release in Brazil.

  - Indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings of ~$(3) billion under U.S. GAAP; additional taxes not practicable to estimate.
  - Tax incentives/reduced rates: benefits of ~$27 million (2022 and 2021) and $33 million (2020), including Vietnam benefits of $18 million (2022), $16 million (2021, 2020).
  - Pre-tax income by geography: 2022 U.S. $22 million, Non-U.S. $(191) million; 2021 U.S. $622 million, Non-U.S. $(1,686) million; 2020 U.S. $(135) million, Non-U.S. $623 million.
  - Uncertain tax positions:
    - Unrecognized tax benefits: $107 million (2022), $122 million (2021), $458 million (2020); 2021 reduction largely from settlement of U.S. 2017 exam on TCJA transition tax (booked at 35%, benefit realized at 21%).
    - Expected net decrease within 12 months: $0–$10 million.
    - Interest and penalties amounts and expense/benefit disclosed; multiple jurisdictions open for examination with varying years (notably U.S. federal 2017–2022).
    - Company notes potential for material impacts to future ETR and net income depending on audit outcomes.

- Held-for-sale and dispositions (Note 24)
  - Held-for-sale:
    - Mong Duong (Vietnam): 2020 agreement to sell 51% interest terminated; assets reclassified from held-for-sale to held and used (Eurasia SBU).
    - Jordan (IPP1/IPP4): agreement to sell 26% interest for $58 million; expected close in 2023; plants remain held-for-sale with $164 million carrying value; AES to retain 10% and account under equity method post-close (Eurasia SBU). Pre-tax income attributable to AES from Jordan: $(6) million (2022), $21 million (2021), $20 million (2020).
  - Dispositions:

    - Alto Maipo (Chile): deconsolidated following Chapter 11 filing in November 2021; pre-tax loss on deconsolidation of $2,074 million, including $224 million goodwill allocation from AES Andes; retained investment recognized at zero fair value; not treated as discontinued operations (South America SBU).
    - Estrella del Mar I: sold for $6 million in November 2021 (MCAC SBU).

structure.title: Held-for-Sale and Dispositions
structure.heading: Note 24 - Held-for-Sale and Dispositions

structure.summary:

Pre-tax income from held-for-sale businesses (in millions): Jordan: 2022 (6), 2021 21, 2020 20.
